title: Contains Duplicate
desc: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.
hints: Comparing every pair works, but it takes O(n²) time. Can you remember what you have already seen?
A hash set answers 'have I seen this value?' in O(1).
Alternative: sort the array first, then only neighbours can be equal.
editorial: Walk through the array and keep a set of values seen so far. If the current value is already in the set, a duplicate exists. Otherwise add it and move on.
Sorting also works (check adjacent pairs) at O(n log n) time with no extra set, which is a useful trade-off when memory is tight.

title: Valid Anagram
desc: Given two lowercase strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, meaning it uses exactly the same letters the same number of times in any order.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
hints: If the lengths differ, the answer is immediately false.
Two strings are anagrams when every letter has the same count in both.
Only 26 letters exist, so a fixed-size count array is enough.
editorial: Count how many times each letter occurs in s, then walk through t and subtract. If a count would go below zero, t has a letter that s does not have enough of.
Sorting both strings and comparing also works, at O(n log n).

title: Two Sum
desc:
Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target.

Exactly one valid pair exists, and you may not use the same element twice. The indices can be returned in any order.
hints: Checking all pairs is O(n²). What if, for each number, you looked up the number you still need?
For x, the partner is target - x.
Store each value's index in a hash map as you scan, and check the map before inserting.
editorial: Scan left to right with a map from value to index. For the current value x, if target - x is already in the map, you found the pair. Otherwise store x and continue.
Checking before inserting guarantees you never pair an element with itself, and the whole thing is a single pass.

title: Valid Parentheses
desc:
Given a string s made only of the characters ( ) [ ] { }, return true if it is valid.

A string is valid when every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, and brackets close in the correct order.
hints: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed.
That last-in, first-out behaviour is exactly what a stack gives you.
At the end the stack must be empty, otherwise some bracket was never closed.
editorial: Push every opening bracket on a stack. When you see a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener; pop it, or return false if it does not match or the stack is empty.
After the scan the stack must be empty. Leftover openers mean unclosed brackets.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day, once.

Return the maximum profit you can make. If no profit is possible, return 0.
hints: Trying every buy/sell pair is O(n²).
For a fixed selling day, the best buying day is the cheapest day before it.
Keep the lowest price seen so far while scanning.
editorial: Scan once, tracking the minimum price so far. At each day, the best profit selling today is price - minSoFar. Keep the maximum of those.
This is a tiny sliding-window idea: the left edge is the cheapest day, the right edge is today.
solution:
def maxProfit(prices):
    best = 0
    low = prices[0]
    for p in prices:
        low = min(low, p)
        best = max(best, p - low)
    return best

title: Binary Search
desc:
Given an array nums sorted in ascending order with distinct values, and an integer target, return the index of target, or -1 if it is not present.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: All values are distinct and sorted ascending
hints: A linear scan is O(n). The array being sorted lets you do much better.
Look at the middle element. Is the target in the left half or the right half?
Keep two boundaries lo and hi and shrink them until they cross.
editorial: Compare the middle element with the target. If equal, return it. If the middle is smaller, the target can only be on the right, so move lo past mid; otherwise move hi before mid.
Each step halves the search range, so at most about log2(n) steps are needed. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 in C++/Java to avoid overflow.

title: Climbing Stairs
desc:
You are climbing a staircase with n steps. Each move you can climb either 1 or 2 steps.

Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.
hints: Think about the very last move. From which steps could you have arrived at step n?
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
Plain recursion repeats work exponentially. Remember results, or just keep the last two.
editorial: To land on step n, your last move was from step n-1 (a 1-step) or from n-2 (a 2-step). So ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), which is the Fibonacci sequence.
Compute it bottom-up, keeping only the previous two values. A naive recursive version without memoization takes exponential time and will time out for n = 45.

title: Majority Element
desc:
Given an integer array nums of length n, return the value that appears more than n / 2 times.

The input is guaranteed to contain such a value, so there is always exactly one answer. A solution that uses O(1) extra space is possible.
constraints: A value occurring more than nums.length / 2 times always exists
hints: Counting every value with a hash map works. Can you do it without the map?
The majority value outnumbers all the other values put together.
Keep one candidate and a counter: same value as the candidate adds one, a different value subtracts one, and a counter of zero lets the next element become the candidate.
editorial: Use the Boyer-Moore voting idea. Hold a candidate and a counter. For each element, if the counter is zero take the element as the new candidate; then add one if it equals the candidate and subtract one otherwise. Every subtraction cancels one majority element against one non-majority element, and since the majority has more than half of all elements, it is the one left standing.

A hash map of counts is simpler and also O(n) time, at the cost of O(n) space. Sorting the array and reading the middle element works too, because the majority value must cover the middle position, but it costs O(n log n).

title: Single Number
desc:
In the integer array nums, every value appears exactly twice except for one value that appears exactly once. Return that single value.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
constraints: Exactly one value appears once; all others appear exactly twice
hints: A hash set or a count map solves it, but uses O(n) memory.
What happens when you combine a number with itself using XOR (^)? And with 0?
XOR is commutative and associative, so XOR-ing the whole array cancels every pair and leaves the single value.
editorial: For any x, x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. XOR also does not care about order. So XOR-ing all elements together makes each pair vanish and leaves exactly the value that has no partner.

The set approach (add on first sight, remove on second) or a sum trick such as 2 * sum(set(nums)) - sum(nums) also works, but both need O(n) extra memory and the sum version can overflow in fixed-width integer types. XOR never overflows.

title: Missing Number
desc:
The array nums holds n distinct integers, each taken from the range 0..n inclusive. That range has n + 1 numbers, so exactly one of them is absent. Return the absent number.

The array may be in any order. Try to use O(1) extra space.
hints: Putting everything in a set and testing 0..n works. Is there a way to avoid the set?
You know which numbers should be there: all of 0..n. Compare that with what is there.
Either subtract sum(nums) from n(n+1)/2, or XOR all indices 0..n together with all values.
editorial: The sum of 0..n is n(n+1)/2. Subtract the sum of the array and the difference is the missing number. In fixed-width languages, the sum stays tiny for n ≤ 10,000, so there is no overflow concern here.

A more overflow-proof variant XORs every index from 0 to n with every array value; each present number appears twice and cancels, leaving the missing one. Sorting and looking for the first index where nums[i] != i also works at O(n log n).

title: Valid Palindrome
desc:
The string s contains letters (upper or lower case), digits and the dash character -. Ignore every dash and ignore the difference between upper and lower case. Return true if what remains reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise return false.

A string with nothing left after ignoring dashes counts as a palindrome.
constraints: s contains only letters, digits and '-'
hints: You could build a cleaned copy and compare it with its reverse. Can you compare in place instead?
Put one pointer at each end and compare the characters they point to.
Before each comparison, move a pointer inward while it sits on a dash. Compare the lower-cased characters.
editorial: Start with i = 0 and j = n - 1. Move i forward while s[i] is a dash, and j backward while s[j] is a dash. If the pointers have not crossed, the lower-cased characters must match; if they do not, return false. Otherwise step both inward and repeat until the pointers meet.

Building the cleaned, lower-cased string and comparing it with its reverse is just as correct and easier to write, but it allocates O(n) extra memory. The two-pointer version uses O(1) extra space and stops at the first mismatch.

title: Is Subsequence
desc:
Return true if string s is a subsequence of string t, and false otherwise.

A subsequence is obtained by deleting zero or more characters from t without changing the order of the characters that remain. The empty string is a subsequence of every string.
constraints: s and t contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Try to match the characters of s inside t one after the other, in order.
Use a pointer i into s. Scan t from left to right.
Whenever t[j] == s[i], advance i. At the end, s is a subsequence exactly when i reached the length of s.
editorial: Walk through t once. Keep an index i of the next character of s still to be matched. If the current character of t equals s[i], matching greedily is always safe, so increment i. If i reaches len(s) every character was matched in order.

Matching each character at its earliest possible position never hurts later characters, which is why the greedy scan is correct. The cost is a single pass over t. (If you had to answer many queries against the same t, you would precompute for each position the next occurrence of each letter instead.)

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
desc:
A staircase has steps numbered 0 to n - 1, and cost[i] is the toll you pay every time you step on step i. You may start on step 0 or on step 1 (paying that step's toll), and from any step you can climb either 1 or 2 steps.

The top of the staircase is the position just past the last step, n. Return the minimum total toll you must pay to reach the top.
hints: Consider the last step you stand on before reaching the top. Which steps could that be?
Let best(i) be the cheapest total toll for a trip that ends by standing on step i (including cost[i]). Then best(i) = cost[i] + min(best(i-1), best(i-2)).
The answer is the cheaper of best(n-1) and best(n-2). You only need the previous two values, so two variables are enough.
editorial: Define best(i) as the minimum toll to stand on step i, tolls included. You can start on step 0 or 1, so best(0) = cost[0] and best(1) = cost[1]. For later steps you arrived from i-1 or i-2, so best(i) = cost[i] + min(best(i-1), best(i-2)). The top can be reached from step n-1 or n-2, so the answer is min(best(n-1), best(n-2)).
Computing it bottom-up while keeping only the last two values uses O(1) extra space. A recursion without memoisation re-solves the same steps over and over and takes exponential time.

title: Pascal's Triangle
desc: Build the first numRows rows of Pascal's triangle and return them as a list of rows. Row i (counting from 0) has i + 1 entries. The first and last entry of every row are 1, and every other entry is the sum of the two entries directly above it in the previous row.
hints: Write out the first five rows on paper and look at how each number relates to the row above.
Row 0 is [1]. For row i, entry j is the sum of entries j-1 and j of row i-1 (treat missing neighbours as 0).
Start every row with 1, add the pairwise sums of the previous row, and end with 1.
editorial: Build the triangle row by row. The new row begins with 1, then for each adjacent pair (prev[j-1], prev[j]) in the previous row it appends their sum, and it ends with 1. This is a direct dynamic program where each row depends only on the row before it.

Another way is the closed form C(i, j) = C(i, j-1) * (i - j + 1) / j, which creates each row without looking at the previous one. For 30 rows every value fits comfortably in a 32-bit integer (the largest is 77,558,760).

title: Plus One
desc:
A non-negative integer is stored as an array digits with the most significant digit first, one digit per element. The number has no leading zeros, except for the number zero itself, which is stored as [0].

Add one to the number and return its digits in the same format. You may not convert the whole array to a single integer, because the number can have thousands of digits.
constraints: digits[0] is not 0 unless the array is exactly [0]
hints: Add one the way you would on paper: start from the last digit.
If the last digit is below 9, just increase it and you are done. If it is 9, it becomes 0 and a carry moves left.
If the carry falls off the front (all digits were 9), the result needs one extra leading 1.
editorial: Scan from the right. Each digit that equals 9 turns into 0 and passes the carry on; the first digit that is not 9 is increased by one and the answer is ready. Usually this stops after a single step.
Only when every digit is 9 does the loop run to the end. The answer is then a 1 followed by all zeros, so we build it directly. The array is processed once, which is optimal.

title: Integer Square Root
desc:
Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down to the nearest integer, that is the largest integer r with r × r ≤ x.

Do not use floating-point numbers, pow, sqrt or any similar built-in.
hints: Trying r = 0, 1, 2, ... until r² exceeds x works, but how many steps is that for large x?
The condition 'r × r ≤ x' is true for small r and false for large r. That is a sorted yes/no pattern you can binary search.
Search r between 0 and x. Compare mid with x / mid instead of multiplying, so that mid × mid cannot overflow a 32-bit integer.
editorial: The predicate r*r ≤ x is monotone: true up to the answer, false afterwards. Binary search for the last r where it holds. For x ≥ 1 the answer is at most x, and a safe test that avoids overflow is mid ≤ x / mid using integer division.

Newton's iteration r = (r + x / r) / 2 converges even faster, in a handful of steps, but needs care with the stopping rule. The linear scan is only fine for tiny x because the answer can be as large as 46,340.

title: First Unique Character
desc:
Given a string s, find the first character that occurs exactly once in the whole string and return its index (0-based). If every character repeats, return -1.

For example, in "planet" every letter is unique, so the answer is 0; in "aabcb" the answer is 3; in "abab" the answer is -1.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Checking each character against all the others works, but is slow for long strings. What do you need to know about each character?
You only need to know how many times each letter occurs in the entire string.
Make one pass to count the letters, then a second pass from the left to return the first index whose letter has count 1.
editorial: Count the occurrences of every character with a hash map (or an array of 26 counters) in one pass. Then scan the string from the left a second time and return the first index whose character has a count of exactly one. If the scan ends without a hit, return -1.

Comparing every character with every other character is O(n²) and becomes slow at 50,000 characters. The two-pass counting approach is linear, and the counter table has constant size because the alphabet is fixed.

title: Isomorphic Strings
desc:
Two strings s and t of the same length are isomorphic if you can rename the characters of s to get exactly t. A renaming assigns each distinct character of s one replacement character, and two different characters of s are never given the same replacement. The order of the characters is preserved.

For example "egg" and "add" are isomorphic (e→a, g→d), but "foo" and "bar" are not (the two os would need different replacements), and neither are "ab" and "cc" (two characters would share one replacement).

Return true if the strings are isomorphic.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Walking both strings together, each character of s must always meet the same character of t.
That one direction is not enough: "ab" vs "cc" passes it. The rule must also hold when you look from t back to s.
Keep two maps, s→t and t→s, and return false as soon as either one is contradicted.
editorial: Scan both strings at the same index. Store, for the pair (a, b), that a maps to b and that b maps back to a. If a was already mapped to something other than b, or b was already the image of something other than a, the strings are not isomorphic.

An equivalent trick is to normalise each string by replacing every character with the index of its first occurrence, and compare the two normalised sequences. Both approaches run in linear time; the mapping tables have at most 36 entries because of the alphabet.

title: Run-Length Compressed Length
desc:
A run is a maximal block of equal consecutive characters. To compress a string, replace every run by its character followed by the length of the run written in decimal, except that a run of length 1 is written as just the character (no number).

For example "aaabccdddd" is compressed to "a3bc2d4", and a run of twelve x characters becomes "x12". Return the length of the compressed string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: You do not have to build the compressed string; its length is enough.
Split the string into runs. A run of length 1 contributes 1; a longer run contributes 1 plus the number of decimal digits of its length.
Scan with two indices: start a run at i, advance j while s[j] == s[i], add the contribution, then continue from j.
editorial: Walk through the string and find each run with a pair of indices. A run of length k costs one character for the letter, plus len(str(k)) more characters when k > 1. Summing over all runs gives the answer in a single linear pass.

Note that counts with several digits matter: a run of 10 to 99 letters adds two digits, 100 to 999 adds three, and so on. Forgetting this is the most common mistake. Building the output string explicitly also works, but wastes memory.
solution:
def compressedLength(s):
    total = 0
    n = len(s)
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        j = i
        while j < n and s[j] == s[i]:
            j += 1
        run = j - i
        total += 1
        if run > 1:
            total += len(str(run))
        i = j
    return total

title: Longest Palindrome by Rearranging
desc:
You are given a string s. Pick some of its characters (each character of s can be used at most once) and arrange them in any order to form a palindrome. Return the maximum possible length of such a palindrome.

For example, from "abccccdd" you can build "dccaccd" of length 7. From "abc" you can only build a single-character palindrome, so the answer is 1.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: In a palindrome, every character appears on both sides of the centre, except possibly one in the middle.
A character that occurs c times can contribute c characters if c is even, or c - 1 of them as pairs if c is odd.
If any character was left over (some count was odd), one of them can sit in the middle, adding 1.
editorial: Count every character. Each character contributes 2 * (count // 2) characters to the two halves of the palindrome. Add up those pair contributions. If the total is smaller than len(s), at least one character has an odd count and has one unused copy, so one of those can be placed in the centre and the answer is the total plus one.
Equivalently, the answer is len(s) minus the number of characters with an odd count, plus one if that number is positive. No actual arrangement needs to be built.

title: Search Insert Position
desc:
You are given a strictly increasing array nums and an integer target. Return the index at which target is found. If it is not present, return the index where it would have to be inserted so that the array stays sorted.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: nums is sorted in strictly increasing order (no duplicates)
hints: A linear scan finds the first element that is not smaller than the target, but it is too slow for the intended bound.
The answer is the number of elements strictly smaller than target. Because the array is sorted, those elements form a prefix.
Binary search for the first index whose value is ≥ target. Keep the search range half-open, [lo, hi), and return lo when it closes.
editorial: The insertion point is the first index i with nums[i] ≥ target, or n when no such index exists. This is a classic lower bound search. The predicate nums[i] ≥ target is false for a prefix and true for the rest, so we can binary search for the boundary.

Keep lo = 0, hi = n. While lo < hi, take mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if nums[mid] < target move lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid. When the loop ends lo is the boundary. Each step halves the range, giving O(log n) time and O(1) space.

title: Move Zeroes
desc:
Given an integer array nums, move every 0 to the end while keeping the relative order of the non-zero values unchanged. Return the resulting array.

Try to do the rearrangement in a single pass with O(1) extra space, by working in place on the array you were given.
hints: Collecting the non-zero values into a new list and padding with zeros works, but uses extra memory.
Use a write pointer that marks where the next non-zero value belongs. Everything before it is already final.
Scan with a read pointer. Whenever nums[read] is non-zero, swap it with nums[write] and advance write.
editorial: Keep two pointers. write is the position where the next non-zero element must be placed; read scans the array. When nums[read] != 0, swap it into nums[write] and advance write. All indices below write hold the non-zero values seen so far, in their original order, and everything between write and read is a zero.
Swapping (rather than copying and then filling with zeros) means each element is touched a constant number of times and zeros drift to the right automatically. Time is O(n), space O(1).

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
desc:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. Remove the duplicates so that every distinct value appears exactly once, keeping the values in order. Return the resulting array.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space by overwriting the array in place.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Equal values are adjacent because the array is sorted, so a duplicate is just an element equal to its predecessor.
Keep a slow pointer at the end of the deduplicated prefix and a fast pointer that scans ahead.
When nums[fast] differs from nums[slow], advance slow and copy the value there. The answer is the first slow + 1 elements.
editorial: Since equal values are grouped together, each new distinct value is the first element after a run of equal ones. Let slow point at the last value kept. For each fast from 1 onward, if nums[fast] != nums[slow] then it is a new value: increment slow and write nums[fast] into that slot.

At the end the first slow + 1 positions hold the distinct values in order. The array is scanned once, so time is O(n); only two indices are used, so space is O(1) beyond the returned slice. Remember to handle the empty array.

title: Number of 1 Bits
desc:
Given a 32-bit signed integer n, return how many bits are set to 1 in its 32-bit two's complement representation.

For example, 11 is 00000000000000000000000000001011, which has three set bits, and -1 has all 32 bits set.
constraints: Negative numbers use the 32-bit two's complement representation
hints: Look at the lowest bit with n & 1, then shift right and repeat. How many times do you need to repeat?

Negative numbers are a trap in some languages: an arithmetic right shift keeps the sign bit, so the loop may never reach zero. Limit the loop to 32 steps, or first convert to an unsigned 32-bit value.
The expression n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Count how many times you can apply it before reaching zero.
editorial: The simplest method inspects each of the 32 bit positions: test (n >> i) & 1 for i from 0 to 31 and add up the results. Because the loop runs exactly 32 times, negative inputs need no special care.

A faster trick is Brian Kernighan's: n & (n - 1) removes exactly the lowest set bit, so repeating it until the value becomes zero takes as many steps as there are set bits. First mask the value to 32 bits (n & 0xFFFFFFFF) so negative numbers behave like their unsigned counterparts.
solution:
def hammingWeight(n):
    n &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1
        count += 1
    return count

title: Happy Number
desc:
Start with a positive integer n. Repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. For instance, 19 becomes 1² + 9² = 82, then 8² + 2² = 68, and so on.

If this process eventually reaches 1, the number is happy. Otherwise it runs forever in a cycle that never contains 1. Return true if n is happy and false if not.
hints: Simulate the process. The difficulty is knowing when to stop for an unhappy number.
The sequence either reaches 1 or repeats a value it has visited before. A hash set of seen values detects the repeat.
After the first step the value is small (at most 810 for a 10-digit number), so a cycle must appear quickly. You can also detect it with slow and fast pointers and no extra memory.
editorial: Define next(x) as the sum of squared digits of x. A 10-digit number is mapped to at most 10 * 81 = 810, and every later value stays small, so the sequence lives in a tiny range. Hence it must either hit 1 (and then stay at 1) or enter a cycle.

Store each visited value in a set and stop when you reach 1 (answer true) or see a value again (answer false). To save memory, use Floyd's tortoise and hare: advance a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps; if they meet at a value other than 1 there is a cycle.

title: Last Stone Weight
desc:
You have a pile of stones, where stones[i] is the weight of the i-th stone. Play the following game until at most one stone remains:

  • Take the two heaviest stones, with weights x ≤ y.
  • If x == y, both stones are destroyed.
  • Otherwise the stone of weight x is destroyed and the other becomes a stone of weight y - x.

Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if no stones remain.
hints: Each round needs the two largest values. Re-sorting the whole array every round works but is slow.
A max-heap gives you the largest element in O(log n) and lets you insert new elements just as fast.
Pop two stones, push their difference back if it is non-zero, and stop when fewer than two stones remain.
editorial: Keep all weights in a max-heap. While at least two stones remain, pop the heaviest two, and if they differ push back their difference. Each round removes at least one stone, so there are fewer than n rounds, each costing O(log n).
Python's heapq is a min-heap, so store negated weights. Sorting the array every round is simpler but costs O(n² log n) overall.

title: Find the Town Judge
desc:
A town has n people labelled 1 to n. Rumour says one of them is the secret judge. If the judge exists, then:

  • the judge trusts nobody, and
  • everybody else trusts the judge.

You are given trust, where each entry [a, b] means that person a trusts person b. Anyone not listed as trusting someone trusts nobody.

Return the label of the judge, or -1 if there is no person who satisfies both rules.
constraints: trust[i] = [a, b] with 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n and a ≠ b
All pairs in trust are distinct
hints: The judge is the only person who can satisfy both rules, so at most one answer exists.
Think of each trust pair as a directed edge a → b. What do the in-degree and out-degree of the judge look like?
Keep one counter per person: subtract one when they trust someone and add one when someone trusts them. The judge ends with exactly n - 1.
editorial: Treat every pair as a directed edge from a to b. The judge has out-degree 0 and in-degree n - 1. Keep a single array score: decrement score[a] and increment score[b] for every pair.

A person who trusts anyone has a score of at most n - 2 (they cannot be trusted by everybody else and also trust someone). The judge scores exactly n - 1. So scan the array and return the person with score n - 1, or -1 if nobody has it. Because pairs are distinct, no one can be counted twice.

title: Unique Paths
desc:
A robot stands in the top-left cell of an m x n grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. In one move it can step either one cell down or one cell to the right; it can never leave the grid.

Return the number of different routes the robot can take. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Look at the last move of any route. From which two cells can the robot arrive at the bottom-right cell?
Let ways[r][c] be the number of routes to cell (r, c). Then ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1].
The first row and first column each have exactly one route. You only need the previous row to compute the next one, so one array of size n is enough.
editorial: Every route to cell (r, c) ends with a step from above or from the left, and those two groups of routes are disjoint. Hence ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1], with the first row and first column equal to 1.

Because each row only depends on the row above, a single array updated left to right does the job: row[c] += row[c-1]. That is O(m · n) time and O(n) space. A route is also just a choice of which m - 1 of the m + n - 2 moves go down, giving the closed form C(m + n - 2, m - 1).

title: Product of Array Except Self
desc:
Given an integer array nums, return an array answer where answer[i] is the product of all elements of nums except nums[i].

Do not use division, and solve it in O(n) time.
constraints: Every prefix and suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Without division, think about what is on the left of i and what is on the right.
answer[i] = (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i).
Fill the answer with left products in one pass, then multiply in the right products in a second pass, going backwards.
editorial: First pass: answer[i] holds the product of all elements before i (running prefix). Second pass from the right: multiply answer[i] by the running product of all elements after i.
Division fails when the array contains zeros, which is why this prefix/suffix trick is the standard answer. Extra space beyond the output array is O(1).
solution:
def productExceptSelf(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return out

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
desc:
Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like 4, 5, 6, 7) that can be formed from its values. The run does not have to appear in order inside the array.

Aim for O(n) time.
hints: Sorting works in O(n log n). Can you avoid it?
Put everything in a set. A number starts a run only if x - 1 is not in the set.
From each run start, count upward while y + 1 is in the set. Each number is visited once overall.
editorial: Store all numbers in a hash set. For every number x whose predecessor x - 1 is missing, x is the start of a run. Walk x, x+1, x+2, ... as long as they are in the set and track the longest length.
Although there is a nested loop, each element is only walked over as part of one run, so the total work is O(n).

title: Maximum Subarray
desc: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) with the largest sum, and return that sum.
hints: Checking every subarray is O(n²) at best.
At each position, decide: extend the previous subarray, or start fresh here.
Starting fresh is better exactly when the running sum so far is negative.
editorial: Let cur be the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index. Then cur = max(x, cur + x): either extend or restart. The answer is the maximum cur seen anywhere.
This is Kadane's algorithm, a one-line dynamic program. Initialise with the first element, not 0, so all-negative arrays work.

title: 3Sum
desc:
Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] from different positions such that a + b + c = 0.

The answer must not contain duplicate triplets. The order of triplets and the order inside a triplet do not matter.
hints: Three nested loops are O(n³). Fix one number and the problem becomes Two Sum.
Sort the array first. Then for a fixed first number, move two pointers inward from both ends.
To avoid duplicates, skip repeated values for the first number and after each found triplet.
editorial: Sort the array. For each index i (skipping equal neighbours), use lo = i + 1 and hi = n - 1. If the sum is too small, move lo right; too large, move hi left; if zero, record it and move lo past duplicates.
Sorting costs O(n log n) and the double loop is O(n²), so the total is O(n²).

title: Container With Most Water
desc:
You are given an array height where height[i] is the height of a vertical line at position i. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water.

Return the maximum amount of water a container can store. The container cannot be tilted.
hints: The water between lines i < j is min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i).
Start with the widest container (first and last line). How can you possibly improve it?
Moving the taller line inward can never help, because the shorter line still limits the height. Move the shorter one.
editorial: Use two pointers at both ends. Compute the area, then move the pointer at the shorter line inward. Moving the taller line only reduces the width without any chance to raise the limiting height, so the best answer is never lost.
Each step shrinks the range by one, so the loop is O(n).

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
desc:
Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character.

A substring is a contiguous part of the string.
hints: Checking every substring is O(n²) or worse.
Keep a window [start, i] that always has unique characters.
When s[i] already occurred inside the window, move start just past its previous position.
editorial: Store the last index where each character was seen. Move the right edge one character at a time. If the character was last seen inside the current window, jump the left edge to just after that index.
The window never moves backwards, so each character is processed once: O(n). An empty string returns 0.

title: Daily Temperatures
desc: Given an array temperatures of daily temperatures, return an array answer where answer[i] is the number of days you must wait after day i to get a warmer temperature. If there is no future warmer day, answer[i] is 0.
hints: For each day, scanning forward is O(n²) in the worst case.
Days still waiting for a warmer day form a pile; the newest waiting day is on top.
Keep a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures. A warmer day resolves everything colder on top of the stack.
editorial: Maintain a stack of indices whose temperatures are in decreasing order (they are still waiting). For the current day i, while the top of the stack has a lower temperature, pop it as j and set answer[j] = i - j. Then push i.
This is the classic monotonic stack: every index is pushed and popped at most once.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
desc:
A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated at an unknown pivot, for example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] became [4,5,6,7,0,1,2].

Given the rotated array nums and an integer target, return the index of target, or -1 if it is not there. Your algorithm must run in O(log n).
hints: Even though the whole array is not sorted, one half around the middle always is.
Compare nums[lo] with nums[mid] to find which half is sorted.
Then check whether the target lies inside the sorted half's range; if yes go there, otherwise go to the other half.
editorial: At every step, at least one of [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is sorted. If nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] the left half is sorted: if the target is within [nums[lo], nums[mid]) search left, else right. Otherwise the right half is sorted, and the same check applies.
Each iteration halves the range, so the total is O(log n).

title: Koko Eating Bananas
desc:
Koko has piles[i] bananas in the i-th pile and h hours before the guards return. Each hour she picks one pile and eats k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer than k, she eats all of it and wastes the rest of the hour).

Return the minimum integer eating speed k so that she finishes all bananas within h hours.
constraints: The total hours can exceed a 32-bit int, so use long / long long in C++ and Java
hints: If speed k works, any larger speed also works. That monotonic behaviour is the key.
The answer lies between 1 and the largest pile.
Binary search on k. To test a speed, sum ceil(pile / k) over all piles and compare with h.
editorial: Binary search on the answer instead of on the array. For a candidate speed mid, hours needed is sum(ceil(p / mid)). If it fits within h, try a smaller speed (hi = mid); otherwise a bigger one (lo = mid + 1).
Total time is O(n log max(piles)). Use 64-bit integers for the hour total because it can exceed 2<sup>31</sup>.

title: Merge Intervals
desc:
Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges, sorted by start.

Intervals that only touch, like [1,4] and [4,5], count as overlapping.
hints: It is hard to merge intervals that are in random order. What order makes it easy?
Sort by start. Then an interval can only overlap with the last merged one.
If start ≤ lastEnd, extend lastEnd to the larger end; otherwise begin a new interval.
editorial: Sort the intervals by start. Keep a result list; for each interval, if its start is at most the end of the last result interval they overlap, so set that end to max(lastEnd, end). Otherwise append it as a new interval.
Sorting dominates the cost: O(n log n).

title: Coin Change
desc:
You have coins of different denominations in coins and an integer amount. Each coin can be used any number of times.

Return the fewest coins needed to make exactly amount, or -1 if it is impossible.
hints: A greedy 'always take the largest coin' fails, for example coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6.
Let dp[a] be the fewest coins for amount a. How does dp[a] relate to smaller amounts?
dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over all coins c ≤ a. Start with dp[0] = 0.
editorial: Build a table dp[0..amount]. For each amount a and each coin c ≤ a, a candidate is dp[a - c] + 1. Initialise unreachable states with a large sentinel (such as amount + 1) and convert it to -1 at the end.
There are amount × coins transitions, so O(amount × n) time. Plain recursion without memoization is exponential.

title: Number of Islands
desc:
You are given a 2D grid of 1s (land) and 0s (water). An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically.

Return the number of islands.
hints: Treat each land cell as a node connected to its 4 neighbours.
When you find an unvisited land cell, you found a new island. Mark the whole island as visited.
Use DFS or BFS (with an explicit stack or queue to avoid deep recursion) to flood the island.
editorial: Scan every cell. Whenever you meet land that has not been visited, increase the island count and flood fill from it (DFS or BFS), marking every connected land cell as visited so it is never counted again.
Each cell is visited a constant number of times, so the time is O(rows × cols). An iterative flood fill avoids recursion-depth problems on large islands.

title: Subsets
desc:
Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set), including the empty subset and the full array.

The solution set must not contain duplicate subsets. You can return the subsets in any order.
hints: For every element you have exactly two choices: include it or skip it.
That is a decision tree of depth n with 2<sup>n</sup> leaves.
Recurse over the index. After exploring 'include', undo the choice (backtrack) before exploring 'skip'.
editorial: Use recursion on the index i with a current list. At i == n, record a copy of the current list. Otherwise first skip nums[i]; then include it, recurse, and remove it again (backtracking).
There are 2<sup>n</sup> subsets and copying each costs up to n, so O(n · 2<sup>n</sup>) time. That is unavoidable because the output itself has that size.
solution:
def subsets(nums):
    res = []
    def go(i, cur):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(cur[:])
            return
        go(i + 1, cur)
        cur.append(nums[i])
        go(i + 1, cur)
        cur.pop()
    go(0, [])
    return res

title: Top K Frequent Elements
desc:
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k distinct values that occur most often in nums. The values may be returned in any order.

The input is chosen so that the answer is unique: the k-th most frequent value occurs strictly more often than the next most frequent value (if there is one). Your running time should be better than O(n log n).
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct values in nums
The k-th most frequent value is strictly more frequent than the (k+1)-th, so the answer is unique
hints: First work out how many times each value occurs. A hash map does that in one pass.
Sorting the distinct values by count costs O(d log d). Notice that a count is never larger than n, the length of the array.
Make an array of buckets where bucket c holds every value that occurs exactly c times, then read the buckets from c = n down to 1 until you have collected k values.
editorial: Count occurrences with a hash map. Then use bucket sort on the counts: create n + 1 lists and put each value into the list indexed by its count. Walk the lists from the largest index downward and append values to the answer until it contains k of them. Every step is linear, so the total is O(n).

A min-heap of size k over (count, value) pairs gives O(n log k), which is better when k is small and the number of distinct values is large. Sorting all distinct values by count is the simplest approach at O(n log n).

title: Two Sum II (Sorted Input)
desc:
The array numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order. Find the two elements at different positions whose sum equals target, and return their 1-based positions [i, j] with i < j.

Exactly one such pair of positions exists. Use only O(1) extra space.
constraints: Exactly one pair of positions i < j has numbers[i] + numbers[j] = target
hints: A hash map would work, but it needs extra space and ignores that the array is sorted.
Look at the smallest and the largest element together. Is their sum too small, too large, or just right?
Put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if too large, move the right pointer left.
editorial: Keep lo = 0 and hi = n - 1. If numbers[lo] + numbers[hi] equals the target, return the 1-based positions. If it is smaller, the element at lo cannot belong to any pair with a partner at or before hi (even the largest partner is not enough), so move lo right. If it is larger, symmetrically move hi left.

Every step discards one index, so the scan is O(n) time with two integer variables of extra space. Binary searching the partner of each element is O(n log n), and a hash map is O(n) time but O(n) space; the two-pointer sweep is the only one that is both fast and constant-memory.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
desc:
An array of distinct integers that was sorted in ascending order has been rotated: some number of elements from the front were moved to the back, keeping their order. For example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] rotated by 4 becomes [5,6,7,0,1,2,4]. A rotation by 0 leaves the array unchanged.

Given the rotated array nums, return its minimum value. Your solution must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: nums is a sorted array rotated by some amount between 0 and nums.length - 1
hints: Scanning for the smallest value is O(n). The sorted structure should let you skip half of the array each time.
Compare the middle element with the last element. Which side of the middle can the minimum be on?
If nums[mid] > nums[hi] the minimum is strictly to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.
editorial: Maintain a range [lo, hi] that is guaranteed to contain the minimum. Look at mid. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the rotation point lies between mid and hi, so the minimum is to the right: set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise the segment from mid to hi is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or earlier: set hi = mid. When lo equals hi, that index holds the minimum.

The range halves every step, giving O(log n). Comparing with nums[hi] instead of nums[lo] avoids a special case for arrays that were not rotated at all. Distinct values matter: with duplicates the comparison can be a tie and the halving argument breaks down.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
desc:
You are given a string s of uppercase letters and an integer k. In one operation you may pick any position of s and change its letter to any other uppercase letter. You may perform at most k operations in total.

Return the length of the longest substring that can be made to consist of one single repeated letter using at most k operations.
constraints: s contains only uppercase English letters
hints: Try every substring and ask how many letters would have to change to make it uniform.
For a window, the cheapest target letter is the one that already appears most often. The cost is window length - highest letter count.
Grow a window to the right. Whenever its cost exceeds k, shrink it from the left. The longest window that was ever valid is the answer.
editorial: A window is valid when length - maxCount ≤ k, where maxCount is the count of its most frequent letter. Slide the right edge across the string, adding letters to a 26-entry count table. While the window is not valid, remove the left letter and advance the left edge. Record the largest valid window length.

Each index enters and leaves the window at most once and a validity check costs at most 26 operations, so the total is O(26 n), i.e. linear. Because windows only shrink when invalid, the left edge never moves backwards. A known refinement keeps maxCount from ever decreasing, saving the 26-step scan, but the straightforward version is easier to trust.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
desc:
Given a positive integer target and an array nums of positive integers, return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target.

If no subarray reaches the target, return 0.
hints: Checking every subarray works in O(n²). The fact that all numbers are positive is a big clue.
Adding an element on the right can only increase the sum; removing one from the left can only decrease it.
Expand the right edge until the sum reaches the target, then shrink from the left as long as the sum still reaches it, recording the length each time.
editorial: Use a sliding window with a running sum. For each new right index add nums[right]. While the sum is at least the target, record right - left + 1, subtract nums[left] and advance left. The best recorded length is the answer, or 0 if none was recorded.

Positivity is what makes the window monotone: with negative numbers shrinking the window could increase the sum and the method fails. Each index enters and leaves once, so the work is O(n). A prefix-sum array with binary search for each right edge gives O(n log n) and also works.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
desc:
Given an integer array nums (negative numbers and zeros are allowed) and an integer k, return how many contiguous, non-empty subarrays have a sum equal to k.

Subarrays at different positions count separately even if they hold the same values.
hints: Trying all start and end positions gives O(n²) subarrays. Think about prefix sums.
The sum of nums[i..j] equals prefix[j+1] - prefix[i].
While scanning, for the current prefix sum P, add the number of earlier prefixes equal to P - k. Keep a hash map from prefix value to how often it occurred.
editorial: Let P_j be the sum of the first j elements. A subarray ending at index j sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals P_j - k. Scan once, keep a map of prefix-sum frequencies (seeded with prefix 0 occurring once for the empty prefix), and add map[P - k] to the answer before recording the current prefix.

A sliding window does not work here because negative values break monotonicity: extending a window can lower the sum. The prefix-sum map is O(n) time and O(n) space. The brute force over all pairs of boundaries is O(n²) with running sums.

title: House Robber
desc:
A row of houses lines a street, and nums[i] is the amount of money inside house i. If you rob two houses that are next to each other, the alarm goes off, so you must never rob two adjacent houses.

Return the maximum amount of money you can rob in one night. If there are no houses, the answer is 0.
hints: For each house you either rob it or skip it. What does robbing it forbid?
Let best(i) be the most you can get from houses 0..i. Then best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i]).
Each value depends only on the previous two, so two variables replace the whole table.
editorial: Let best(i) be the maximum loot using only the first i+1 houses. Skipping house i leaves best(i-1); robbing it forces you to skip house i-1, giving best(i-2) + nums[i]. Take the larger. The answer is the value for the last house, or 0 for an empty street.

Because only the last two values are ever needed, the table collapses to two variables and the space drops to O(1). The same idea works as a top-down recursion with memoisation, but the loop is shorter and avoids recursion depth limits.

title: Jump Game
desc:
You stand on index 0 of an array nums. When you are on index i you may jump forward any number of positions from 1 up to nums[i] (or not at all if nums[i] is 0).

Return true if you can reach the last index, and false otherwise.
hints: Exploring every possible jump sequence is exponential. What do you really need to know at each index?
Positions you can reach always form one contiguous block starting at index 0, so only the furthest reachable index matters.
Scan left to right, keeping far. If you ever stand at an index greater than far, you are stuck; otherwise update far = max(far, i + nums[i]).
editorial: Keep far, the furthest index reachable so far. For each index i, if i > far then index i can never be reached and the answer is false. Otherwise extend far with i + nums[i]. If far ever reaches the last index we can stop with true.

Why contiguous? If you can reach index k, you can reach everything below k by shorter jumps from the same earlier position, so reachable indices never have holes before the furthest one. A dynamic program that marks each reachable index works too, but costs O(n²) in the worst case.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
desc:
Given an integer array nums, return the length of its longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence keeps the original order of elements but may skip some of them, and strictly increasing means every chosen value is larger than the one before it.

An O(n²) solution is easy; try to reach O(n log n).
hints: Let L(i) be the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i. How does it relate to earlier indices?
L(i) = 1 + max(L(j)) over all j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]. That is the O(n²) solution.
For O(n log n), keep tails[k], the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. It stays sorted, so each new number can be placed with binary search.
editorial: Maintain a sorted list tails where tails[k] is the smallest tail value among all increasing subsequences of length k+1 seen so far. For each number x, find the first position whose value is ≥ x (binary search). If there is none, append x (a longer subsequence now exists); otherwise overwrite that slot with x, which makes a tail smaller or equal and never hurts. The answer is the length of tails.

Note that tails itself is not a valid subsequence, only its length is meaningful. Searching for the first value ≥ x (not > x) is what makes the subsequence strictly increasing. The simple DP over all pairs needs O(n²) time, which is too slow for 10,000 elements in a browser.

title: Decode Ways
desc:
A message made of letters has been encoded as digits using the mapping A = 1, B = 2, ..., Z = 26. Given the digit string s, count in how many different ways it can be decoded back into letters.

Every group of digits you decode must be exactly one of the codes 1 to 26 written without a leading zero, so 06 is not a valid code and a lone 0 cannot be decoded. For example 11106 can be read as 1 1 10 6 or 11 10 6 but not as anything that uses 06. If there is no valid decoding, return 0. Because the count can be huge, return it modulo 1,000,000,007.
constraints: s contains only the digits 0-9 (it may start with 0)
hints: Look at the end of the string. The last letter came from either the last digit or the last two digits.
Let ways(i) be the number of decodings of the first i digits. The last digit contributes ways(i-1) if it is not '0'; the last two digits contribute ways(i-2) if they form a number from 10 to 26.
Each value needs only the previous two, so keep two variables. Apply the modulo after every addition.
editorial: Let ways(i) be the number of decodings of the first i characters, with ways(0) = 1 (the empty prefix). The i-th character alone is a valid code when it is not '0', adding ways(i-1). The pair of characters ending at i is valid when it lies between "10" and "26", adding ways(i-2). Everything is taken modulo 1,000,000,007, and the answer is ways(n).

A top-down recursion on the suffix with memoisation gives the same recurrence, but recursion depth would reach 5,000. A string such as "0" or "30" gives 0 because the zero can never be attached to a valid code, and the recurrence handles that automatically: both branches contribute nothing.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
desc:
Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence is obtained by deleting zero or more characters from a string without changing the order of the characters that remain.

If the strings share no characters, the answer is 0.
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Compare the last characters of the two strings. What if they are equal? What if they differ?
Let L(i, j) be the answer for the first i characters of text1 and the first j of text2. If the characters match, L(i, j) = L(i-1, j-1) + 1; otherwise L(i, j) = max(L(i-1, j), L(i, j-1)).
Fill an (m+1) x (n+1) table row by row. Row 0 and column 0 are all zeros. Only the previous row is needed, which saves memory.
editorial: Use a table where dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of text1 and the first j of text2. When the two last characters are equal they can both be matched, giving dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. When they differ, at least one of them is unused, so take max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). The answer is dp[m][n].

Each row depends only on the one above, so two rows of length n+1 are enough, reducing space from O(m · n) to O(n). Brute force over all subsequences of one string is exponential. The table approach performs about 2.25 million cell updates at the maximum size, well within limits.

title: Insert Interval
desc:
You are given a list of closed intervals [start, end] that is sorted by start and contains no two intervals that share a point (for consecutive intervals, end of one is strictly smaller than start of the next). You are also given one more interval newInterval = [start, end].

Insert newInterval into the list. Merge every interval that overlaps with it, where two intervals that only share an endpoint, such as [1, 3] and [3, 5], also count as overlapping. Return the resulting list, sorted by start and again free of overlaps.
constraints: 0 ≤ start ≤ end ≤ 100,000 for every interval, including newInterval
intervals is sorted by start, and each interval's end is strictly smaller than the next interval's start
hints: The existing intervals fall into three groups relative to the new one: entirely before it, overlapping it, and entirely after it.
Copy every interval whose end is smaller than newInterval's start. Then, while the next interval's start is at most newInterval's end, absorb it by widening newInterval.
Append the widened newInterval, then copy the remaining intervals unchanged. Because the input is sorted, one pass is enough.
editorial: Walk through the sorted list once in three phases. Phase one copies intervals that end before the new interval starts. Phase two merges every interval that starts no later than the new interval's end: set the new start to the smaller start and the new end to the larger end. Phase three appends the merged interval followed by all the intervals that remain, which all start after it ends.

Using ≤ when comparing a start with the current end is what makes intervals that merely touch merge together. Inserting then re-sorting and merging the whole list also works, but costs O(n log n) while the sorted input lets us finish in O(n).

title: Meeting Rooms II
desc:
Each meeting is described by a pair [start, end): it begins at time start and finishes at time end. The meetings are given in no particular order.

Return the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two meetings held in the same room overlap. A meeting that ends at time t does not clash with a meeting that starts at time t, so they can share a room. If there are no meetings, return 0.
hints: The number of rooms you need is the largest number of meetings that are happening at the same moment.
Separate the start times from the end times and sort each list.
Sweep through the starts in order. If the earliest unfinished meeting has already ended (its end ≤ this start), reuse its room; otherwise open a new room.
editorial: Sort all start times and all end times independently. Use two pointers: for each start time s in order, if the smallest remaining end time is ≤ s, a room has been freed, so advance the end pointer (reuse the room); otherwise we need an additional room. The number of times we could not reuse a room is the answer.

Alternatively keep a min-heap of end times of the meetings in progress: sort meetings by start, pop the heap top if it is ≤ the new start, then push the new end. The heap size at the end is the answer. Both run in O(n log n); the two-sorted-lists version avoids the heap.

title: Permutations
desc:
Given an array nums of distinct integers, return every possible ordering of its elements. Each ordering uses all the numbers exactly once.

Return the orderings as rows in any sequence you like, but the numbers inside a row must appear in the order of that arrangement (so [1,2] and [2,1] are two different rows).
hints: With n distinct numbers there are n! orderings, so you will need to build them one at a time.
Fill the positions from left to right. At each position, try every number that has not been used yet.
Keep a used flag per element. Choose a number, mark it, recurse to the next position, then unmark it (backtrack).
editorial: Build an arrangement position by position. At depth d, loop over all indices; if the number is unused, append it, mark it used and recurse. When the arrangement has n numbers, store a copy. After the recursive call returns, remove the number and clear the flag so the next candidate can take its place.

An alternative is to swap elements in place: at depth d, swap nums[d] with each nums[j] for j ≥ d, recurse, and swap back. That avoids the used array. Either way there are n! results and each costs O(n) to copy, which matches the output size.
solution:
def permute(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    res = []
    used = [False] * n
    cur = []

    def go():
        if len(cur) == n:
            res.append(cur[:])
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            cur.append(nums[i])
            go()
            cur.pop()
            used[i] = False

    go()
    return res

title: Combination Sum
desc:
You are given an array candidates of distinct positive integers and a positive integer target. Return every unique collection of candidates whose sum is exactly target. A candidate may be used any number of times in one collection.

Two collections are the same if they use each candidate the same number of times, so list every collection only once, with its numbers in non-decreasing order (for example [2,2,3], never [2,3,2]). The rows can be returned in any order. If nothing works, return an empty array.
constraints: The answer has fewer than 500 combinations
hints: Think of building a combination one number at a time, with a running total that must reach target.
To avoid listing the same multiset in different orders, only allow choosing candidates at the current index or later.
Sort the candidates. In the recursion, loop from the current index; if a candidate overshoots the remaining amount, every later candidate does too, so stop.
editorial: Sort the candidates, then recurse with the start index and the remaining amount. When the remaining amount hits zero, record the current list. Otherwise try each candidate from the start index onward, recurse with the same index (reuse is allowed), and remove it again afterwards. Because indices never go backwards, every combination is produced exactly once in non-decreasing order.

Sorting lets you break out of the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds what is left, which prunes many branches. The cost is bounded by the number of nodes in the search tree, roughly O(n<sup>target / min</sup>) in the worst case. A dynamic-programming table of combinations per sum also works, but it stores many partial lists, so backtracking is the usual choice.
solution:
def combinationSum(candidates, target):
    cands = sorted(candidates)
    res = []
    cur = []

    def go(start, left):
        if left == 0:
            res.append(cur[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(cands)):
            c = cands[i]
            if c > left:
                break
            cur.append(c)
            go(i, left - c)
            cur.pop()

    go(0, target)
    return res

title: Rotate Image
desc:
You are given a square n × n matrix of integers. Return a new matrix that is the original turned 90 degrees clockwise.

In the result, the first row is the first column of the input read from bottom to top, the second row is the second column read from bottom to top, and so on. The input itself is left unchanged.
hints: Look at where a single cell lands: the top-left corner of the input becomes the top-right corner of the output.
Work out the target position of matrix[i][j] in terms of i, j and n.
The cell at row i, column j moves to row j, column n - 1 - i. Fill a fresh matrix with that rule.
editorial: After a clockwise quarter turn, the old row i becomes the new column n - 1 - i, and the old column j becomes the new row j. So result[j][n - 1 - i] = matrix[i][j]. Allocate an n × n result and copy every cell once.

Doing it in place is a classic follow-up: transpose the matrix (swap [i][j] with [j][i]) and then reverse every row, or rotate four cells at a time layer by layer. Since this version asks for a new matrix, the O(n²) extra space is the simplest, least error-prone choice.

title: Max Area of Island
desc:
A grid contains 1 for land and 0 for water. An island is a set of land cells that are linked through neighbours directly above, below, left or right of each other (diagonals do not link cells).

The area of an island is the number of land cells in it. Return the largest area among all islands, or 0 when the grid has no land.
hints: Each land cell is a node; its land neighbours in the four directions are connected to it.
When you reach an unvisited land cell, explore its whole island while counting how many cells you touch.
Use an explicit stack or queue (BFS/DFS) and mark cells as visited when you push them, so a 100 × 100 island does not overflow the call stack.
editorial: Scan the grid. At every land cell that has not been seen, start a flood fill with a stack, marking cells visited as they are pushed, and count the cells popped. The count is that island's area; keep the maximum over all islands (start at 0 for a grid without land).

Every cell enters the stack at most once, so the running time is O(rows × cols). A recursive DFS is shorter to write but can reach depth 10,000 on a snake-shaped island; a disjoint-set union that tracks component sizes is another valid approach.

title: Rotting Oranges
desc:
Each cell of a grid is 0 (empty), 1 (a fresh orange) or 2 (a rotten orange). Every minute, each fresh orange that touches a rotten orange directly above, below, left or right becomes rotten. All oranges that qualify turn at the same moment.

Return the number of minutes that pass until no fresh orange is left. If some fresh orange can never rot, return -1. If there is no fresh orange at the start, the answer is 0.
hints: Rot spreads outwards at the same speed from every rotten orange, like ripples. Time equals distance.
Start from all rotten oranges at once rather than one at a time.
Run a BFS with all rotten cells in the queue at minute 0, process it level by level (one level per minute), and count the fresh oranges you convert. If any fresh orange remains, the answer is -1.
editorial: Put every rotten cell in a queue and count the fresh oranges. Process the queue one level at a time: for each cell in the current level, rot its fresh neighbours, decrease the fresh counter and add them to the next level. The number of levels that actually rotted something is the elapsed time. If the counter is not zero at the end, some fresh orange was cut off by empty cells and the answer is -1.

This is a multi-source BFS: the time for a cell to rot is its shortest distance to the nearest rotten orange. Simulating each minute by rescanning the whole grid also works, but it can take O(R · C) per minute and up to O((R · C)²) overall, whereas BFS touches every cell only once.

title: Course Schedule
desc:
A school offers numCourses courses numbered 0 to numCourses - 1. Each entry prerequisites[i] = [a, b] says that course b must be completed before you can take course a. The same pair may appear more than once, and a pair may even name the same course twice.

Return true if it is possible to complete every course, and false otherwise.
constraints: Duplicate pairs and pairs with a = b are allowed
hints: Draw an edge from b to a for every pair. When can the courses not all be finished?
Exactly when the graph has a cycle, because every course on a cycle waits for another course on it. A pair [a, a] is a cycle of length one.
Repeatedly take a course with no unmet prerequisites (in-degree 0), remove it, and lower the in-degree of its dependants. If you remove every course, there is no cycle.
editorial: Count, for every course, the number of prerequisite edges pointing at it (duplicates count each time, which is fine because they are removed each time too). Put all courses with count 0 in a queue. Pop a course, mark it finished and decrement the count of each course that depends on it, queueing those that reach 0. The answer is true exactly when all courses were popped (Kahn's algorithm).

A DFS that colours nodes white/grey/black and reports a cycle when it meets a grey node is equivalent. Prefer the queue-based version here, since a chain of 1,000 courses would give a recursion depth of 1,000 for DFS. Both run in O(V + E).
solution:
from collections import deque


def canFinish(numCourses, prerequisites):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
    indeg = [0] * numCourses
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        adj[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(numCourses) if indeg[i] == 0)
    done = 0
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        done += 1
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return done == numCourses

title: Network Delay Time
desc:
A network has n nodes numbered 1 to n. Each entry times[i] = [u, v, w] is a one-way link: a message sent from node u reaches node v after exactly w time units. There may be several links between the same two nodes.

At time 0 a message is sent from node k, and every node forwards it along all of its outgoing links the moment it first receives it. Return the time at which the last node receives the message, or -1 if some node never gets it.
hints: A node gets the message at the earliest time over all routes, so you need the shortest travel time from k to each node.
The answer is the largest of those shortest times, or -1 if some node cannot be reached at all.
Weights are positive, so Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap gives all shortest times in O((V + E) log V).
editorial: Build an adjacency list. Keep a distance array initialised to infinity with dist[k] = 0 and a min-heap of (distance, node). Pop the closest node; if the popped distance is stale (bigger than the recorded one), skip it. Otherwise relax each outgoing edge and push improved distances. When the heap is empty, the answer is the maximum distance, or -1 if any node is still at infinity.

Bellman-Ford (relax all edges up to n - 1 times) is simpler and also correct for positive weights, but it costs O(V · E), which is 300,000 steps in the worst case here. Dijkstra is the intended solution because it scales to much larger graphs.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring Length
desc:
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Given a string s, return the length of the longest contiguous substring of s that is a palindrome.

For example, for "babad" the answer is 3 ("bab" or "aba"), and for "cbbd" the answer is 2 ("bb").
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Testing every substring for being a palindrome takes O(n³) time. Can a palindrome be grown instead of tested?
Every palindrome has a centre: a character (odd length) or the gap between two characters (even length). Growing outwards from a centre keeps it a palindrome as long as the two new ends match.
Try all 2n-1 centres, expand while the characters at both ends are equal, and keep the best length.
editorial: Expand around centres. For each index i consider the odd-length palindromes centred at i and the even-length palindromes centred between i and i+1. Start with lo and hi at the centre and move them outwards while s[lo] == s[hi]; the length of the last valid window is hi - lo - 1 after the loop. The maximum over all centres is the answer.

There are 2n-1 centres and each expansion costs up to O(n), giving O(n²) total, which is fast for n = 2,000. Manacher's algorithm reduces this to O(n), and dynamic programming over (i, j) pairs gives the same quadratic time with quadratic memory.
solution:
def longestPalindromicSubstringLength(s):
    n = len(s)
    best = 1
    for centre in range(2 * n - 1):
        lo = centre // 2
        hi = lo + centre % 2
        while lo >= 0 and hi < n and s[lo] == s[hi]:
            lo -= 1
            hi += 1
        best = max(best, hi - lo - 1)
    return best

title: Count Palindromic Substrings
desc:
Given a string s, count how many of its contiguous substrings are palindromes. Substrings are counted by their position, so two equal substrings taken from different places are counted separately.

For example, "aaa" has 6 palindromic substrings: three single "a", two "aa" and one "aaa". The string "abc" has 3.
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: There are about n²/2 substrings. Checking each one from scratch costs another factor of n.
If the substring from i to j is a palindrome, then growing it by one matching character on each side gives another palindrome.
Take each of the 2n-1 centres (a character or a gap between two), expand while both ends match, and count one palindrome per successful expansion.
editorial: Every palindrome has a unique centre, which is either a single character or the gap between two adjacent characters. For each of the 2n-1 centres, expand outwards while the two end characters are equal; each successful step reveals one more palindromic substring, so you add one to the counter per step.

This takes O(n²) time in the worst case (a string of identical characters) and O(1) space. A DP table is_pal[i][j] also works but needs O(n²) memory. The count can reach about two million, which fits easily in 32 bits.
solution:
def countPalindromicSubstrings(s):
    n = len(s)
    total = 0
    for centre in range(2 * n - 1):
        lo = centre // 2
        hi = lo + centre % 2
        while lo >= 0 and hi < n and s[lo] == s[hi]:
            total += 1
            lo -= 1
            hi += 1
    return total

title: Count Anagram Windows
desc:
Given a text s and a pattern p, count the substrings of s that are anagrams of p. A substring is an anagram of p if it has the same length as p and contains exactly the same characters with the same multiplicities (in any order). Substrings are counted by their starting position, so overlapping matches all count.

For example, with s = "cbaebabacd" and p = "abc" the matching windows start at indices 0 (cba), 6 (bac), so the answer is 2. With s = "aaaa" and p = "aa" the answer is 3. If p is longer than s the answer is 0.
constraints: s and p consist of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Sorting every window of length p.length and comparing with sorted p is correct but slow for big inputs.
Consecutive windows differ by one character leaving and one entering. Maintain character counts instead of recomputing them.
Keep the difference between the needed counts and the window counts, and track how many characters have a non-zero difference. A window matches when that number is zero.
editorial: Slide a window of length m = len(p) over s. Store, for each character, need[c] - window[c], and keep a counter of how many characters currently have a non-zero value. Adding the new character on the right and removing the old one on the left each update one entry and possibly change the counter by one. Whenever the counter is zero, the window is an anagram of p.

Each step does constant work, so the total time is O(n + m). Recomputing counts from scratch for every window costs O(n · m), and sorting each window O(n · m log m), both too slow when both strings are around 30,000 characters long.

title: Minimum Deletions: All A's Before B's
desc:
You are given a string s made only of the letters a and b. You may delete any characters you like. After the deletions, the remaining string must be ordered: no b may appear before an a (so it looks like aaa...abbb...b, and either part may be empty).

Return the minimum number of characters you must delete. For example "aababbab" needs 2 deletions, and "bbaaaaabb" needs 2. A string that is already ordered needs 0.
hints: In the final string there is a split point: only a's on the left of it and only b's on the right.
For a fixed split, you must delete every b on the left and every a on the right. Try all n+1 splits using prefix counts.
It can also be done in one pass: keep bCount and best. On 'b' increase bCount; on 'a', set best = min(best + 1, bCount).
editorial: Fix a split position. Everything left of it should be a and everything right should be b, so the cost is the number of b's on the left plus the number of a's on the right. Computing this for every split with a running count of b's and a total count of a's gives an O(n) solution with a single minimum over the splits.

The one-pass dynamic-programming form is more compact. Let best be the minimum deletions to order the prefix seen so far, and b the number of b's seen. A new b can always be appended (just increment b). A new a either gets deleted (best + 1) or forces all earlier b's to be deleted (b), so best = min(best + 1, b).

title: Find First and Last Position of Target
desc:
Given an array nums sorted in non-decreasing order, find where the value target starts and ends. Return [first, last], the lowest and highest indices holding target. If target does not occur, return [-1, -1].

The solution must run in O(log n) time, so scanning outward from a match is not good enough when there are many duplicates.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: One binary search can find some index holding the target, but with many duplicates that index tells you little about the edges.
Run two binary searches that each look for a boundary: the first index with value ≥ target and the first index with value > target.
The range is [lower, upper - 1]. If lower == upper (or lower is out of bounds) the target is absent.
editorial: Define lowerBound(x) as the first index whose value is ≥ x, or n if none. The first occurrence of target is lowerBound(target) provided that index is in range and holds the target. The index after the last occurrence is lowerBound(target + 1), so the last occurrence is that minus one.

Both bounds come from the same binary search routine, so the total cost is two O(log n) searches. Be careful that target + 1 can exceed the 32-bit range in fixed-width languages; implementing an upper bound with a strict nums[mid] ≤ target test avoids that.

title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days
desc:
A conveyor belt carries packages with the given weights, in the order they arrive. Each day the ship loads packages in that order, without reordering and without exceeding its weight capacity, then sails. A package cannot be split across days.

Return the smallest ship capacity that lets all packages be shipped within days days.
hints: Try a fixed capacity: how would you count the number of days it needs? Load greedily and start a new day when the next package no longer fits.
If a capacity works, any larger capacity works too, so feasibility is monotonic in the capacity.
Binary search the capacity between max(weights) (the heaviest single package must fit) and sum(weights) (ship everything in one day), using the greedy count as the test.
editorial: The capacity must be at least the heaviest package and is never worth more than the total weight.
