For a candidate capacity, simulate greedily: keep adding packages to the current day until the next one would overflow, then begin a new day. Greedy loading uses the fewest possible days for that capacity.

Since a larger capacity never needs more days, the predicate "fits within days" flips from false to true exactly once. Binary search the smallest capacity where it is true. There are about log(sum) iterations, each costing O(n), for O(n log(sum)) time and O(1) space.

title: Max Consecutive Ones III
desc: You are given a binary array nums (every element is 0 or 1) and an integer k. You may flip at most k zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive ones you can obtain.
hints: Instead of thinking about flipping, ask: what is the longest subarray that contains at most k zeros?
A window with too many zeros can be repaired by shrinking it from the left; a valid window can be extended on the right.
Expand right one step at a time, counting zeros. While the count exceeds k, move left forward (decrementing the count if the dropped element was a zero). Track the largest window.
editorial: Flipping at most k zeros inside a stretch is possible exactly when that stretch contains at most k zeros. So the answer is the length of the longest subarray with at most k zeros.

Use a sliding window. Add nums[right], and if it is a zero increase the zero count. If the count passes k, advance left until the count is back to k. After each step, the window [left, right] is valid, so update the best length. Each index enters and leaves the window at most once: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
desc:
Each interval is a pair [start, end] with start < end. Two intervals overlap when they share more than a single point, so intervals that merely touch, such as [1, 2] and [2, 3], do not overlap.

Return the minimum number of intervals you have to remove so that the remaining intervals are pairwise non-overlapping.
hints: Removing the fewest intervals is the same as keeping the largest possible set of mutually compatible intervals.
When choosing which interval to keep first, the one that finishes earliest leaves the most room for the rest.
Sort by end value. Sweep through, keeping an interval whenever its start is at least the end of the last kept interval; otherwise count it as removed.
editorial: This is the classic activity-selection problem. Maximise the number of intervals kept; the answer is n - kept.

Greedy rule: sort by end and always keep the interval that ends first among those compatible with what you already kept. An exchange argument shows this is optimal: any optimal solution can swap its first interval for the earliest-ending one without creating a conflict. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the sweep is O(n); extra space is for the sorted copy.

title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
desc:
Balloons are pinned to a wall. Balloon i covers the horizontal range [points[i][0], points[i][1]] (both ends included). An arrow shot straight up from position x bursts every balloon whose range contains x, and the arrow keeps going.

Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons.
hints: Balloons whose ranges share a common point can be burst by a single arrow.
Sort the balloons by their right end. Shooting at the right end of the first balloon is never worse than shooting anywhere else inside it.
Shoot at the current right end; every following balloon whose left end is ≤ that position is already burst. The first balloon whose left end is larger needs a new arrow, placed at its own right end.
editorial: Sort balloons by right end. Place the first arrow at the right end of the first balloon: any arrow that bursts that balloon can be slid right to its end without losing any other balloon that is later in the sorted order, so this position is at least as good as any other.

Walk through the sorted list. A balloon with start ≤ arrowPos is already burst. Otherwise fire a new arrow at its right end and continue. Since both ends are inclusive, a balloon that starts exactly at the arrow position is hit. Comparisons only (no sums) keep the logic safe at the 32-bit limits. O(n log n) for sorting, O(1) beyond that.

title: Car Fleet
desc:
Several cars drive along a one-lane road towards a destination at mile target. Car i starts at mile position[i] and moves at a constant speed[i] miles per hour. All starting positions are distinct and lie before the destination.

A car can never pass the car in front of it. If it catches up, it slows down and from then on travels at the speed of that car, bumper to bumper; together they form a fleet. A single car is also a fleet, and a car that catches up exactly at the destination still joins the fleet that arrives there.

Return the number of fleets that arrive at the destination.
constraints: 0 ≤ position[i] < target, and all positions are distinct
hints: Process the cars from the one closest to the destination backwards. A car's fate depends only on the cars in front of it.
For each car compute the time it would need if the road were empty: (target - position) / speed. A car with a time not larger than the fleet ahead of it will merge into that fleet.

Go in descending order of position and keep the arrival time of the fleet in front (a stack, or just its top). A car whose time is strictly larger starts a new fleet. Compare fractions by cross-multiplying to avoid rounding.
editorial: Sort cars by starting position, nearest to the destination first. The first car is always the head of a fleet. For each next car, compute its free-road arrival time t = (target - p) / s. If t is not larger than the arrival time of the fleet immediately ahead, it catches up (or ties exactly at the finish) and joins it; its effective time becomes the fleet's time. If t is strictly larger, it will never catch that fleet and becomes the head of a new one.

Only the time of the closest fleet ahead matters, which is the top of a monotonic stack of fleet times (strictly increasing from the front car backwards). To stay exact, compare (target - p1) / s1 > (target - p2) / s2 as (target - p1) * s2 > (target - p2) * s1; the products are at most 1012, which needs 64-bit arithmetic in some languages. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
solution:
def carFleet(target, position, speed):
    cars = sorted(zip(position, speed), reverse=True)
    fleets = 0
    lead_dist = lead_speed = None
    for p, s in cars:
        d = target - p
        # strictly later than the fleet ahead: d / s > lead_dist / lead_speed
        if lead_dist is None or d * lead_speed > lead_dist * s:
            fleets += 1
            lead_dist, lead_speed = d, s
    return fleets

title: Gas Station
desc:
There are n gas stations arranged in a circle. Station i sells gas[i] units of fuel, and driving from station i to the next station (i + 1) % n burns cost[i] units.

You begin at some station with an empty tank, fill up there, and then drive clockwise, refuelling at every station you reach. You complete the circuit if the tank never goes below zero on the way and you arrive back at the starting station. Return the smallest starting index from which you can complete the circuit, or -1 if no start works.
hints: Trying every start and simulating the lap costs O(n²). Look for structure that lets you skip many starts at once.
If the total gas is smaller than the total cost, the answer is -1 straight away. Otherwise some start works.
Sweep once, keeping a running tank. When the tank drops below zero at station i, none of the starts between the previous candidate and i can work, so restart the candidate at i + 1.
editorial: If sum(gas) < sum(cost), no start works. Otherwise a valid start exists, and a single sweep finds it. Keep a running tank from a candidate start. If the tank becomes negative after station i, then starting at any station between the candidate and i would have reached i with at most as much fuel, and would fail too. So the next candidate is i + 1 and the tank resets.

The candidate left at the end of the sweep is the answer. It is also the smallest valid index, because it is the first position where the prefix sum of gas[i] - cost[i] reaches its global minimum. The sweep is O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

title: Jump Game II
desc:
You stand on index 0 of the integer array nums. From index i you may jump forward by any distance from 1 to nums[i] (so a value of 0 means you cannot move from there).

Return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index. The input is built so that the last index is always reachable.
constraints: The last index is reachable from index 0
hints: A DP where dp[i] is the fewest jumps to reach i works, but is O(n²) in the worst case.
Think of the indices reachable with 1 jump, then with 2 jumps, and so on. Each group is a contiguous range, like levels of a BFS.
Track the end of the current range and the farthest index reachable from anything inside it. When you pass the end of the range, take a jump and extend the range to the farthest point.
editorial: Treat the array as an implicit graph and run BFS, noticing that the set of indices reachable in exactly k jumps forms a contiguous block. Keep cur_end, the last index reachable with the jumps taken so far, and far, the farthest index reachable by one more jump from any index seen so far.

Scan from left to right, updating far = max(far, i + nums[i]). When i reaches cur_end you must jump again: increment the counter and set cur_end = far. Stop the scan before the last index. This greedy is O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Spiral Matrix
desc: Given an m x n integer matrix, return all of its elements in a single flat array, reading them in clockwise spiral order: start at the top-left cell, go right along the top row, then down the right column, then left along the bottom row, then up the left column, and keep spiralling inwards until every cell has been visited once.
constraints: Every row has exactly n elements
hints: Picture four edges of a rectangle that you peel off one at a time. How do the edges change after each full loop?
Maintain four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. After walking along an edge, move that boundary one step inwards.
Be careful when only one row or one column is left: after walking the top row and the right column, check that top ≤ bottom and left ≤ right before walking back, or you will read cells twice.
editorial: Keep four indices top, bottom, left, right bounding the unvisited rectangle. Repeat while top ≤ bottom and left ≤ right: read the top row left to right and increment top; read the right column top to bottom and decrement right; if rows remain, read the bottom row right to left and decrement bottom; if columns remain, read the left column bottom to top and increment left.

The two guards before the last two edges handle matrices that collapse to a single row or column in the middle of the walk. Each cell is appended once, so the running time is O(m * n) and the extra space beyond the output is O(1). An alternative is to simulate the walk with a visited grid and turn right whenever the next cell is blocked.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
desc:
Given an m x n integer matrix, whenever a cell contains 0, set every cell in its entire row and its entire column to 0. Return the resulting matrix.

All decisions are based on the original matrix: zeros created by this process must not cause further rows or columns to be cleared. Aim for O(1) extra space beyond the matrix itself.
hints: First collect the rows and columns that contain a zero in the original matrix, and only then start writing zeros.
Two arrays, one boolean per row and one per column, are enough. Can you store those flags inside the matrix itself?
Use the first row and first column as the flag storage. Remember separately whether the first row and the first column originally contained a zero, since they are overwritten by the markers.
editorial: The straightforward approach records which rows and which columns contain a zero in two arrays of size m and n, then does a second pass clearing every cell whose row or column is flagged. That uses O(m + n) extra space.

To get O(1) extra space, reuse the first row and first column as the flag arrays. Before anything else, note whether row 0 and column 0 contain a zero. Then scan the rest of the matrix and, on seeing a zero at (i, j), set matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j] to 0. Next clear every cell (i, j) with i, j ≥ 1 whose row marker or column marker is 0. Finally clear the first row and first column if they were flagged at the start.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
desc:
You are given points, a list of [x, y] coordinates on a plane, and an integer k. Return the k points that are closest to the origin (0, 0) by straight-line (Euclidean) distance.

The points may be returned in any order. The input is built so that the set of k closest points is unique: when k < n, the k-th closest point is strictly closer than the (k+1)-th closest.
constraints: The answer set is unique (no tie at the boundary of the k-th and (k+1)-th closest)
hints: Sorting all points by distance and taking the first k works in O(n log n). You do not need the full order, though.
You can compare squared distances x*x + y*y, so no square root or floating point is needed.
Keep a max-heap of size k holding the best points seen so far, keyed by distance. If a new point is closer than the heap's top, replace the top.
editorial: Compare squared distances to avoid floating point arithmetic. The simplest solution sorts the points by squared distance and slices the first k, in O(n log n).

A heap does better when k is small: maintain a max-heap (keyed by squared distance) containing at most k points. For every new point, push it; if the heap grows beyond k, pop the farthest point. After scanning all points the heap holds the k closest, in O(n log k) time and O(k) space. Quickselect can reach O(n) on average.

title: Task Scheduler
desc:
A CPU must run every task in tasks, where equal numbers mean tasks of the same type. Each unit of time the CPU either runs one task or sits idle. The tasks may be executed in any order, but two tasks of the same type must be separated by at least n units of time (so after running a task of some type, the next task of that type may start no earlier than n + 1 time units later).

Return the minimum total number of time units needed to finish all the tasks, counting idle units.
hints: Only the number of tasks of each type matters, not their order in the input. Start by counting them.
Greedy idea: in each window of n + 1 time units, run the most frequent remaining types, one task of each distinct type.
Use a max-heap of remaining counts. In every round pop up to n + 1 types, run one task of each, push back those with tasks left, and add n + 1 to the time unless this was the final round.
editorial: Count the tasks of each type and put the counts in a max-heap. Time is processed in rounds of n + 1 units. In a round, pop up to n + 1 of the largest counts (each pop is a different type, so the cooldown is respected), decrement them, and remember those that still have work. After the round push them back. If the heap is non-empty the round consumed all n + 1 units (idle slots included); in the final round only as many units as tasks were run are added.

Always running the types with the most remaining work is optimal because the most frequent type is the bottleneck. There is also a closed form: with m the largest count and c the number of types having that count, the answer is max(len(tasks), (m - 1) * (n + 1) + c).
solution:
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def leastInterval(tasks, n):
    heap = [-c for c in Counter(tasks).values()]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    time = 0
    while heap:
        slots = n + 1
        left = []
        while slots and heap:
            c = heapq.heappop(heap) + 1
            slots -= 1
            if c < 0:
                left.append(c)
        for c in left:
            heapq.heappush(heap, c)
        time += (n + 1) if heap else (n + 1 - slots)
    return time

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
desc:
Given an array nums of positive integers, decide whether it can be split into two groups (every element goes into exactly one group) such that both groups have the same sum.

Return true if such a split exists and false otherwise.
hints: If the total is odd, the answer is immediately no. Otherwise each group must sum to half of the total.
The question becomes: is there a subset of the numbers that adds up to total / 2? Think of a 0/1 knapsack.
Keep a boolean array reach[s] meaning 'some subset sums to s'. For each number x, update sums from high to low: reach[s] |= reach[s - x].
editorial: The two groups sum to the total, so each must sum to total / 2; an odd total makes it impossible. Finding one group with sum target = total / 2 automatically leaves the rest with the same sum.

This is subset-sum. Let reach[s] be true when some subset of the processed numbers adds to s, starting with only reach[0] true. For each number x iterate s from target down to x (downwards so x is used at most once) and set reach[s] |= reach[s - x]. The answer is reach[target]. The sum is at most 20,000, so this is about 200 × 10,000 steps. A big-integer bitmask (bits |= bits << x) performs the same update in one operation per number.

title: Number of Provinces
desc:
There are n cities. Some pairs of cities are directly linked by a road; two cities can also reach each other indirectly through a chain of roads. A province is a maximal group of cities that can all reach one another.

You are given an n x n matrix isConnected where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly linked and 0 means they are not. Every city is linked to itself.

Return the number of provinces.
hints: Cities form an undirected graph. A province is exactly one connected component.
Start a DFS or BFS from any city you have not visited, marking every city you can reach. Each start counts as a new province.
Alternatively use union-find: begin with n separate sets, merge the sets of i and j whenever they are linked, and subtract one from the count each time a merge actually joins two different sets.
editorial: Count connected components of the graph described by the matrix. With union-find, start with n components. For each pair i < j with isConnected[i][j] = 1, find the roots of i and j; if they differ, union them and decrease the component count by one. The final count is the answer.

Use path compression (and optionally union by size) so each find is near constant time. The matrix has n² entries, so reading it dominates: O(n² · α(n)). A DFS or BFS over the matrix rows gives the same bound.

title: Redundant Connection
desc:
A connected, cycle-free graph (a tree) on nodes 1..n had one extra edge added between two nodes that were not already directly connected. You are given the resulting list edges of n undirected edges; edges[i] = [a, b] joins nodes a and b.

Removing a suitable edge turns the graph back into a tree. If several edges could be removed, return the one that appears last in edges. Return it exactly as written in the input (same order of its two numbers).
constraints: edges[i] = [a, b] with 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n and a ≠ b
No two edges join the same pair of nodes
hints: Adding one edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle. The answer lies on that cycle.
Process the edges in order, keeping track of which nodes are already connected. When would an edge be redundant?
Use union-find: for each edge, if both endpoints already share a root, this edge closes the cycle and is the answer; otherwise union them.
editorial: Insert the edges one by one into a union-find structure. For an edge [a, b], find the roots of a and b. If the roots differ, the edge connects two separate pieces, so union them. If the roots are equal, a and b were already connected by earlier edges, so this edge completes the unique cycle.

That edge is also the last cycle edge in the input: every other edge of the single cycle came earlier (it was needed to connect a and b), and edges after it are not on the cycle. So the first edge found to be redundant while scanning in order is the required answer. With path compression this runs in nearly linear time.

title: Combination Sum II
desc:
Given an array candidates of positive integers (values may repeat) and a positive integer target, find every distinct combination of candidates whose sum is exactly target.

Each element of the array may be used at most once, but if a value appears several times in the array it may be picked up to that many times. Two combinations are the same if they contain the same values with the same multiplicities, regardless of which copies were chosen.

Return the combinations as rows with their numbers written in non-decreasing order. The rows can be listed in any order, and no combination may be listed twice. If no combination works, return an empty list.
hints: Sort the array so equal values sit next to each other and each row comes out in non-decreasing order.
Do a depth-first search where each step picks the next element to include, moving forward through the sorted array so no element is reused. Stop when the remaining sum is negative.
To avoid duplicate rows, at any one level of the recursion skip a value if it is equal to the previous value you already tried at that same level.
editorial: Sort the candidates. Recurse with a start index and the remaining target. In the loop over i from start, break as soon as candidates[i] exceeds the remaining target (all later values are at least as large). Otherwise take it, recurse with start i + 1 (each element is used once), and undo.

Duplicates are removed with one rule: inside a single loop, if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1], skip it. The first copy of a value covers every combination that begins with that value at this position, while a later copy at the same level would repeat them. Copies of the same value are still allowed deeper in the recursion because there the index equals the start of the new loop.

title: Shortest Path in a Binary Matrix
desc:
You are given an n x n grid of 0s (open cells) and 1s (blocked cells). A clear path goes from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, visits only open cells, and moves between cells that touch either along a side or at a corner, so each step may go in any of the 8 directions.

The length of a path is the number of cells it visits, including the first and the last. Return the length of the shortest clear path, or -1 if there is none.
constraints: The start or the end cell may itself be blocked, in which case the answer is -1
hints: Every step costs the same, so which classic algorithm finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
Use breadth-first search from the top-left cell, expanding to all 8 neighbours that are in range and open. Don't forget to check that the start cell is open.
Mark a cell as visited when you push it on the queue, and keep the distance with it (or process the queue level by level). The first time you pop the bottom-right cell, its distance is the answer.
editorial: The grid is an unweighted graph where each open cell is connected to up to eight open neighbours, so BFS gives the shortest path. If the start or end cell is blocked, return -1 right away. Put the start in a queue with distance 1 and mark it visited. Pop a cell; if it is the bottom-right cell, return its distance; otherwise push each unvisited open neighbour with distance + 1, marking it visited when pushed.

Marking on push (not on pop) guarantees each cell enters the queue once, and BFS order guarantees the first arrival at any cell is along a shortest route. Total work is O(n²) with 8 neighbour checks per cell. If the queue empties without reaching the target, no clear path exists.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may complete as many buy/sell transactions as you like, subject to these rules:

  • you can hold at most one share at a time, so you must sell before buying again;
  • after you sell, you cannot buy on the very next day (one day of cooldown);
  • a share bought on day i can be sold on any later day.

Return the maximum total profit you can make. If no profitable trade exists, the answer is 0.
hints: At the end of any day you are in one of a few situations: holding a share, not holding and free to buy, or just sold and in cooldown.
Track the best profit for each of the three states and update them day by day: hold = max(hold, free - price), sold = hold_prev + price, free = max(free, sold_prev).
Be careful to use the previous day's values on the right-hand side, so compute new values in a temporary step. The answer is the larger of the 'free' and 'sold' states on the last day.
editorial: Define three values at the end of day i: hold is the best profit while owning a share, sold is the best profit if you sold today (so tomorrow is a cooldown), and free is the best profit while owning nothing and being allowed to buy tomorrow.

Transitions for price p: hold' = max(hold, free - p) (keep, or buy today from the free state); sold' = hold + p (sell today); free' = max(free, sold) (rest, or finish yesterday's cooldown). Start with hold = -infinity, sold = 0, free = 0. After the last day the answer is max(sold, free); ending while still holding a share can never be better. Only O(1) values are kept, so the space is constant.

title: Trapping Rain Water
desc: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where each bar has width 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
hints: Water above a bar is limited by the shorter of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right, minus the bar's own height.
You can precompute 'tallest to the left' and 'tallest to the right' arrays, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
To reach O(1) space: use two pointers and always process the side with the smaller current bar.
editorial: For each index, trapped water = min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height[i]. Two pointers avoid the extra arrays: if height[lo] < height[hi], the left side is the limiting one, so update maxLeft and add the water at lo; otherwise do the symmetrical step on the right.
Both pointers walk inward once: O(n) time, O(1) space. A monotonic stack gives another O(n) solution.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
desc: Given an array heights where each element is the height of a histogram bar of width 1, return the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the histogram.
hints: For each bar, the best rectangle using its full height extends left and right until it meets a shorter bar.
Finding the nearest shorter bar on each side for every position naively is O(n²).
A stack of increasing heights tells you the left boundary; when a shorter bar arrives, pop and compute areas.
editorial: Keep a stack of (start index, height) with increasing heights. When the new bar is shorter than the top, pop the top: it can extend from its start to the current index, so its area is height × (i - start). The popped bar's start becomes the new bar's start, because the new bar can extend left over it.
Appending a sentinel 0 at the end flushes the remaining stack. Every bar is pushed and popped once: O(n).
solution:
def largestRectangleArea(heights):
    stack = []
    best = 0
    for i, h in enumerate(heights + [0]):
        start = i
        while stack and stack[-1][1] >= h:
            idx, height = stack.pop()
            best = max(best, height * (i - idx))
            start = idx
        stack.append((start, h))
    return best

title: Sliding Window Maximum
desc:
You are given an array nums and a window of size k that moves from the far left to the far right, one position at a time.

Return an array containing the maximum value of each window position.
hints: Taking the max of each window directly costs O(n · k).
Elements that are smaller than a newer element to their right can never be a window maximum again.
Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing. The front is always the current maximum.
editorial: Maintain a deque of indices with decreasing values. For each new element, pop from the back while the back value is smaller or equal (they can never win again), then push the new index. Pop from the front if its index has left the window. Once i ≥ k - 1, the front is the maximum of the window.
Each index enters and leaves the deque once: O(n).

title: Minimum Window Substring
desc:
Given two strings s and t, return the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t (including duplicates). If no such substring exists, return the empty string.

The test data guarantees the answer is unique when it exists.
constraints: s and t contain English letters (case-sensitive)
hints: Expand the right end until the window contains everything required.
Then shrink from the left while it still contains everything, recording the smallest window.
Track how many characters of t are still missing using a count map, so you never rescan the window.
editorial: Count the required characters of t. Move the right pointer; a character that is still needed decreases the missing counter. While missing == 0 the window is valid: record it if it is shorter, then move the left pointer and put that character back (if it becomes needed again, missing grows).
Both pointers only move forward, so the algorithm is O(|s| + |t|). Return "" if no valid window was ever found.

title: Edit Distance
desc:
Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations needed to convert word1 into word2.

You may insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character. Each counts as one operation.
constraints: An empty string is written as "" in the input
hints: Compare the last characters of both strings. If equal, they cost nothing.
If they differ you have three choices: insert, delete or replace. Each reduces to a smaller subproblem.
Let dp[i][j] be the distance between the first i characters of word1 and the first j of word2.
editorial: Define dp[i][j] as the edit distance between word1[:i] and word2[:j]. Base cases: dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j. If the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min(dp[i-1][j-1] (replace), dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i][j-1] (insert)).
Only the previous row is needed, so space can be reduced to O(m). Time is O(n · m).

title: N-Queens II
desc:
Place n queens on an n × n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal).

Return the number of distinct solutions.
hints: Place queens one row at a time; each row gets exactly one queen.
Track which columns and diagonals are already occupied so you can reject a square in O(1).
On a diagonal, row - col is constant; on an anti-diagonal, row + col is constant.
editorial: Recurse row by row. For each column in the current row, skip it if the column, the diagonal r - c or the anti-diagonal r + c is taken. Otherwise mark them, recurse to the next row, then unmark (backtrack). Reaching row n means one complete solution.
The search is pruned heavily compared with trying all n<sup>n</sup> placements, and n = 9 finishes instantly.

title: Lower Median of Two Sorted Arrays
desc:
You are given two integer arrays a and b, each sorted in non-decreasing order, and at least one of them is non-empty. Imagine merging them into one sorted array of length m + n.

Return the element of the merged array at 0-based index (m + n - 1) / 2 (integer division). This is the lower median: for an odd total it is the middle element, and for an even total it is the smaller of the two middle elements. Your solution should run in O(log(min(m, n))) time.
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Merging the arrays and indexing is O(m + n). To beat that you cannot look at every element.
Let L = (m + n - 1) / 2 + 1. The answer is the largest of the L smallest elements overall. Suppose you take i of them from a and L - i from b: which condition makes that split correct?

Binary search on i in the shorter array. The split is right when the last taken element of each array is no larger than the first untaken element of the other array. The answer is the larger of the two last taken elements.
editorial: Make a the shorter array. The first L = (m + n - 1) / 2 + 1 merged elements consist of some i elements of a and L - i elements of b. The split is correct exactly when a[i-1] ≤ b[L-i] and b[L-i-1] ≤ a[i] (ignoring indices that fall outside the arrays). Binary search for the smallest i with a[i] ≥ b[L-i-1]; i is limited to [max(0, L - n), min(m, L)] so both counts stay valid. The answer is the larger of a[i-1] and b[L-i-1] that exist.

Searching the shorter array keeps the cost at O(log(min(m, n))). A simpler approach is the two-pointer merge that stops at index L - 1, costing O(m + n). The lower-median definition removes the usual averaging step for even totals, so the result is always an element of one of the arrays and fits in a 32-bit integer.

title: First Missing Positive
desc:
Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest positive integer (1, 2, 3, ...) that does not appear in it. The array may contain negative numbers, zeros, duplicates and huge values.

Your algorithm should run in O(n) time and use only O(1) extra space, so you are allowed to rearrange the array itself.
hints: A set of the values and a loop over 1, 2, 3, ... works, but uses O(n) extra memory.
With n numbers, the answer is always in the range 1..n+1. Values outside 1..n can never matter.
Use the array as its own hash table: try to place each value v in 1..n at index v - 1 by swapping. Afterwards the first index i with nums[i] != i + 1 gives the answer i + 1.
editorial: The answer is at most n + 1, because n numbers cannot cover more than n positive values. So only values in 1..n are interesting. For each position i, while nums[i] is in 1..n and is not already sitting at its home index (nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]), swap it into its home. The duplicate check guarantees termination. Every swap puts one value at its final position, so there are at most n swaps in total.

Then scan once: the first index i where nums[i] != i + 1 means i + 1 is missing; if every index matches, the answer is n + 1. A hash set gives a simpler O(n) time, O(n) space solution; sorting gives O(n log n) with O(1) extra space. The in-place swap method meets both bounds at once by treating array indices as hash buckets.

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
desc:
Given a string s consisting only of the characters ( and ), return the length of the longest contiguous substring that is a well-formed (balanced) bracket sequence.

A sequence is well-formed when every ( has a matching ) later on and every ) has a matching ( before it. The empty string has length 0.
hints: Checking every substring costs O(n²) or O(n³). Think about how a stack finds matching pairs in a single pass.
Push indices of unmatched characters onto the stack, starting with a sentinel -1. A valid run then extends from the index just under the top of the stack up to the current index.
On '(' push its index. On ')' pop; if the stack is now empty, push the current index as the new sentinel, else the run length is i - stack[-1].
editorial: Keep a stack of indices, initialised with -1 as a base. For each '(' push its index. For each ')' pop the top; if the stack becomes empty this ')' is unmatched, so push its index as the new base; otherwise the valid substring ending here starts right after the new top, and its length is i - stack[-1]. The answer is the largest such length.

There is an O(1) space alternative: scan left to right counting '(' and ')' and reset both counters when ')' exceeds '('; record 2 * ')' whenever the counts are equal. Then scan right to left with the roles swapped. A DP over end positions also works, but the stack version is the easiest to get right.

title: Burst Balloons
desc:
There are n balloons in a row, and balloon i is painted with the number nums[i]. You burst all of them one at a time, in an order you choose. Bursting balloon i earns left * nums[i] * right coins, where left and right are the numbers on the nearest balloons that have not burst yet on either side. If there is no such balloon on a side, use 1 for that side.

Return the maximum number of coins you can collect by bursting every balloon. With no balloons, the answer is 0.
hints: Choosing which balloon to burst first splits the row in a way that makes the two parts depend on each other. Try thinking about which balloon is burst last instead.
If balloon k is the last one to burst inside the open range (l, r), its neighbours at that moment are exactly l and r, and the two sides (l, k) and (k, r) are independent subproblems.

Pad the array with a 1 at both ends. Let dp[l][r] be the best total for the balloons strictly between l and r. Then dp[l][r] = max over k of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l]*a[k]*a[r]. Fill by increasing interval length.
editorial: Pad the array: a = [1] + nums + [1]. Define dp[l][r] as the maximum coins from bursting all balloons strictly between indices l and r. Pick k as the balloon that bursts last in that range: at that time only l and r are left beside it, so it yields a[l] * a[k] * a[r], and the balloons on each side were burst earlier within their own independent ranges. So dp[l][r] = max_k (dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l]*a[k]*a[r]), filled by increasing gap r - l. The answer is dp[0][n+1].

Thinking about the first balloon to burst fails because after removing it, its neighbours become adjacent and the subproblems are no longer independent. Choosing the last one fixes this. There are O(n²) ranges and O(n) choices of k each, hence O(n³) in total; with n = 300 and values at most 100 the answer stays well below 2<sup>31</sup>.

title: Regular Expression Matching
desc:
Implement a tiny pattern matcher. Given a text s and a pattern p, return true if the pattern matches the entire text, and false otherwise.

The pattern supports two special characters. . matches any single character. * means "zero or more copies of the element right before it", where that element is either a letter or a .. For example a* matches "", a, aaa, and .* matches any string at all. The pattern is well-formed: a * never appears first and never directly follows another *.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
p contains only lowercase English letters, '.' and '*'
In p, every '*' has a letter or '.' directly before it
hints: Compare the pattern and the text from the front. A plain character or '.' consumes exactly one text character; the interesting case is a '*'.

Let match(i, j) say whether s[i:] matches p[j:]. If p[j+1] is '*', you either skip the pair p[j], p[j+1] entirely, or (when s[i] fits p[j]) consume one text character and stay on the same pattern position.
Fill a table from the ends toward the front, or memoise the recursion. There are only (|s|+1) x (|p|+1) distinct states.
editorial: Define dp[i][j] as true when s[i:] matches p[j:]. The base case is dp[|s|][|p|] = true. For a state, let first be true when i < |s| and p[j] is equal to s[i] or is '.'. If p[j+1] is '*', then dp[i][j] = dp[i][j+2] or (first and dp[i+1][j]): use zero copies, or use one copy and stay on the same starred element. Otherwise dp[i][j] = first and dp[i+1][j+1].

Filling the table from the bottom-right corner needs only two rows at a time. A plain recursion without memoisation repeats the same states exponentially often (patterns like a*a*a*a*b are the classic killer), which is why the table matters. Because the whole text must match, an empty text can still match a pattern like a*b*.

title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
desc:
Given an array nums of positive integers and an integer k, decide whether the numbers can be divided into exactly k non-empty groups so that every group has the same sum. Each element must go into exactly one group.

Return true if such a division exists and false otherwise.
hints: If the total is not divisible by k, or some number is larger than total / k, the answer is immediately false. Otherwise every group must sum to target = total / k.
Fill the groups one after another: pick unused numbers until the current group reaches target, then start the next group.

With at most 16 numbers, the set of used numbers fits in a bitmask. The current group's partial sum is determined by the mask (it is sum(mask) mod target), so you can remember masks from which no solution exists and never explore them again.
editorial: Let target = total / k. Search over bitmasks of used numbers: from a mask, add any unused number that keeps the current group at most target; when the group sum reaches target it resets to zero. If the mask with all bits set is reached, the answer is true. Because the partial group sum depends only on the mask, a mask that failed once can be stored in a set and skipped, so there are at most 2n states, each tried with n choices: O(n · 2n).

Plain backtracking that places each number into one of k buckets can take k<sup>n</sup> steps on unlucky inputs, which is why the memo matters. Sorting the numbers ascending allows an early break as soon as a number does not fit, and skipping a number equal to an unused predecessor avoids retrying identical choices. An equivalent bottom-up DP stores, for each mask, the partial sum of the current group, or -1 if the mask cannot be reached.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
desc:
You are given an integer matrix. Starting from any cell, you may repeatedly step to a cell directly above, below, left or right, as long as the value in the new cell is strictly larger than the value in the current cell. You cannot leave the matrix.

Return the largest number of cells on any such path (a path of a single cell has length 1).
hints: Treat each cell as a node, with an arrow from a cell to every neighbour that holds a larger value. Because values strictly grow, this graph has no cycles.
Define best(cell) as the longest path that starts there. It equals 1 plus the maximum of best(neighbour) over larger neighbours.

Compute it in order of decreasing value, so every larger neighbour is already done. Equivalently, process cells by increasing value and let each cell extend the best path ending at a smaller neighbour.
editorial: Sort all cells by value. Walk through them from smallest to largest; for each cell, len[cell] = 1 + max(len[nb]) over neighbours with a strictly smaller value (those were processed earlier, and equal values never count). The answer is the maximum of len. Sorting makes the order explicit, so there is no recursion at all, which matters for a 100 × 100 snake-shaped matrix where a recursive DFS would go 10,000 levels deep.

A memoised DFS from every cell gives the same result and is shorter to write when recursion depth is not a concern. A third way is a topological sort: peel off cells with no smaller neighbour layer by layer, and the number of layers is the answer. Each approach does O(R · C) work per cell-visit; sorting adds the log factor.

title: Distinct Subsequences
desc:
Given two strings s and t, count in how many different ways t can be obtained as a subsequence of s. A subsequence keeps the original order of the characters it keeps; two ways are different if they use a different set of positions in s, even when the resulting letters are the same.

For example, t = "rabbit" can be picked from s = "rabbbit" in 3 ways (any one of the three bs can be left out), and t = "bag" can be picked from s = "babgbag" in 5 ways. If t cannot be formed, return 0.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
The answer (and every intermediate count in the standard table) fits in a signed 32-bit integer
hints: Enumerating every subsequence of s is exponential. Look at the last character of s and ask how it can be used.

Let ways[i][j] be the number of ways to form the first j characters of t from the first i characters of s. The last character of s is either skipped or, if it equals t[j-1], used as the last character of the match.
ways[i][j] = ways[i-1][j] + (ways[i-1][j-1] if s[i-1] == t[j-1] else 0), with ways[i][0] = 1. The table can be compressed to one row if j is iterated downwards.
editorial: Use dynamic programming over prefixes. Let ways[i][j] be the number of ways the prefix t[:j] is a subsequence of s[:i]. The empty target can be formed in exactly one way (take nothing), so ways[i][0] = 1, and a non-empty target cannot be formed from an empty source, so ways[0][j] = 0 for j > 0. For the general case, either the character s[i-1] is not used, contributing ways[i-1][j], or it is matched with t[j-1] (only possible when they are equal), contributing ways[i-1][j-1].

Each row depends only on the previous one, so a single array of length len(t)+1 suffices as long as the inner loop runs from high j to low j; this avoids using the character s[i-1] twice. Time is O(|s| · |t|), about a million updates for the largest input. Plain recursion without memoisation repeats the same sub-problems and is exponential.

title: Shortest Palindrome Length
desc:
You may add characters only at the front of the string s; nothing can be inserted in the middle or at the end. Find the shortest palindrome you can create this way and return its length.

For example, for s = "aacecaaa" you can prepend a single a to get "aaacecaaa", so the answer is 9. For s = "abcd" you must prepend "dcb" to get "dcbabcd", so the answer is 7. If s is already a palindrome the answer is len(s).
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and digits
hints: Whatever you add is determined by how much of the start of s is already a palindrome.
If the longest palindromic prefix of s has length k, the remaining n - k characters must be mirrored in front, so the answer is 2n - k.

Find k in linear time with the KMP prefix function on s + '#' + reverse(s): the last value of the prefix function is the length of the longest prefix of s that equals a suffix of reverse(s), i.e. a palindromic prefix.
editorial: Let k be the length of the longest prefix of s that is a palindrome. The characters after that prefix cannot be part of the palindromic core, so their reverse must be placed in front, giving a result of length n + (n - k) = 2n - k. Any shorter result would need a longer palindromic prefix, contradicting maximality of k.

Checking every prefix for palindromicity costs O(n²), acceptable only for small inputs. To get O(n), build t = s + '#' + reverse(s) and compute the KMP failure (prefix) function. The final value pi[-1] is exactly k: a prefix of s that matches a suffix of reverse(s) is a prefix that equals its own reversal. The separator keeps the match from crossing the boundary (the alphabet never contains #).

title: Split Array Largest Sum
desc: Split the non-negative integer array nums into exactly k non-empty contiguous pieces. The cost of a split is the largest piece sum. Return the smallest cost that any split can achieve.
hints: A dynamic programming over (prefix, pieces) works but is cubic in the straightforward form. Think about whether the answer itself can be searched for.
Fix a limit L and ask: can the array be cut into at most k pieces, each with sum ≤ L? A greedy sweep that extends each piece as far as possible answers this.

The answer is the smallest feasible L. Feasibility is monotonic, so binary search L between max(nums) and sum(nums). Note that using fewer pieces can always be turned into exactly k by splitting pieces further, which never raises the maximum.
editorial: Let feasible(L) be true when the array can be divided into at most k contiguous pieces with every sum ≤ L. The greedy check scans left to right, closing a piece when adding the next element would exceed L; it uses the minimum possible number of pieces for that limit.

If a limit works, a bigger one works too, so binary search on the answer between max(nums) (every element must fit in some piece) and sum(nums) (one piece). Having fewer than k pieces is fine: because k ≤ n, any piece with more than one element can be cut further without increasing the maximum, until exactly k pieces exist. Complexity is O(n log(sum)) time and O(1) space; a DP would cost O(k n2). Total sums stay below 109, inside 32-bit range.

title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
desc: Given an integer array nums that may contain negative numbers, and a positive integer k, return the length of the shortest non-empty contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k. If no such subarray exists, return -1.
hints: The classic shrinking window fails here because negative values mean that adding an element can lower the sum. Use prefix sums instead: you want the closest pair i < j with pre[j] - pre[i] ≥ k.
For a fixed j, a larger and closer i is always better. If pre[i1] ≥ pre[i2] with i1 > i2, then index i2 is useless.
Maintain a deque of indices with increasing prefix sums. At each j, pop from the front while pre[j] - pre[front] ≥ k (recording lengths), then pop from the back while pre[back] ≥ pre[j], then push j.
editorial: Let pre[0] = 0 and pre[j] = nums[0] + ... + nums[j-1]. We want the minimum j - i with i < j and pre[j] - pre[i] ≥ k.

Keep a deque of candidate start indices whose prefix sums are strictly increasing. When we reach j: (1) while the front index satisfies the condition, record j - front and pop it, since any later j would only give a longer length for that start; (2) while the back index has a prefix sum that is not smaller than pre[j], pop it, since j is a later and lower start that dominates it; (3) push j. Each index is pushed and popped once, so the algorithm runs in O(n) time and O(n) space.

title: Candy
desc:
Children stand in a line, and child i has rating ratings[i]. You must give every child at least one candy, and any child with a strictly higher rating than an adjacent neighbour (left or right) must receive strictly more candies than that neighbour. Equal ratings impose no constraint.

Return the minimum total number of candies you need to hand out.
hints: Handle the two directions separately. First think only about the constraint with the left neighbour.
Sweep left to right: if a child's rating is higher than the left neighbour's, give one more candy than that neighbour, otherwise start at 1.
Do a second sweep from right to left for the right-neighbour constraint, and for each child take the larger of the two requirements. The sum is the minimum.
editorial: The two rules, one about each neighbour, are independent lower bounds. Make an array left where left[i] is the length of the strictly increasing run ending at i (counting i), and an array right with the length of the strictly decreasing run starting at i. Child i needs at least max(left[i], right[i]) candies.

That bound is also sufficient: giving each child exactly the maximum satisfies both neighbour constraints, so it is optimal. Two passes and one extra array give O(n) time. A single pass tracking the lengths of the current up-slope and down-slope reduces the extra space to O(1).

title: IPO
desc:
A company wants to raise its capital before an IPO by completing at most k distinct projects. You start with capital w. Project i yields a pure profit of profits[i] but you may only start it when your current capital is at least capital[i]. Starting a project does not consume capital: when you finish it, its profit is simply added to your capital, and the finished project cannot be repeated.

Projects are done one after another. Return the maximum capital you can have after completing at most k projects.
hints: At every step, which projects are even allowed? Among those, which one would you pick?
Since profit never decreases your capital and capital only unlocks more projects, always picking the most profitable affordable project is safe.
Sort projects by required capital. Sweep a pointer to move every newly affordable project into a max-heap keyed by profit, then pop the best one, add its profit and repeat up to k times.
editorial: Greedy works here because finishing any project only increases capital, and a higher capital can never make an option disappear. So among all currently affordable projects the one with the largest profit is never a worse choice: it gives at least as much capital as any alternative, which unlocks at least as many future projects.

Implementation: sort the projects by capital requirement. For up to k rounds, push every project whose requirement is at most the current capital into a max-heap of profits (advancing a pointer through the sorted list), then pop the top and add it to the capital. If the heap is empty, no project is affordable and you stop. The cost is O(n log n + k log n).
solution:
import heapq

def findMaximizedCapital(k, w, profits, capital):
    projects = sorted(zip(capital, profits))
    heap = []
    i = 0
    n = len(projects)
    for _ in range(k):
        while i < n and projects[i][0] <= w:
            heapq.heappush(heap, -projects[i][1])
            i += 1
        if not heap:
            break
        w -= heapq.heappop(heap)
    return w

title: Number of Islands II
desc:
An m x n map starts as all water. You are given a list positions; the k-th entry [r, c] turns the water cell in row r, column c into land (if that cell is already land, nothing changes).

An island is a maximal group of land cells that are connected through shared sides (up, down, left, right; diagonals do not count).

Return an array whose k-th element is the number of islands right after the k-th operation has been applied.
constraints: positions[k] = [r, c] with 0 ≤ r < m and 0 ≤ c < n
The same cell may appear more than once
hints: Re-running a full flood fill after every operation is far too slow for big inputs. How can you update the count incrementally?
When a cell becomes land it forms a new island (count + 1), but it may then join up to four neighbouring islands.

Use union-find over cell indices r * n + c. After marking the new cell, union it with each land neighbour; every union that merges two different sets lowers the count by one. Skip cells that are already land.
editorial: Keep a union-find over the m * n cells plus a boolean land array and a running island count. For each position: if the cell is already land, just record the current count. Otherwise mark it as land, add one to the count (it is a new island on its own), then look at the four neighbours. For each neighbour that is land, find the two roots; if they differ, union them and subtract one from the count.

Each operation does at most four unions, and with path compression and union by size every find is almost constant time, so the total cost is about O(k · α(m · n)) for k operations, plus O(m · n) to set up. Repeated positions must be ignored: counting them again as new islands would be wrong.

title: Palindrome Partitioning II
desc:
Cut the string s into consecutive pieces so that every piece reads the same forwards and backwards (a palindrome). Each place where you split the string counts as one cut.

Return the minimum number of cuts needed. A string that is already a palindrome needs 0 cuts.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
hints: Every single character is a palindrome, so some answer always exists (at most n - 1 cuts).
Let cuts[i] be the minimum cuts for the first i characters. The last piece s[j..i-1] must be a palindrome, giving cuts[i] = min(cuts[j] + 1) over such j. How can you test palindromes fast?
Instead of testing every substring, expand around each of the 2n-1 centres. Whenever s[l..r] is a palindrome, update cuts[r + 1] = min(cuts[r + 1], cuts[l] + 1).
editorial: Define cuts[i] as the minimum cuts for the prefix of length i, with cuts[0] = -1 so that a prefix that is itself one palindrome costs -1 + 1 = 0. Initialise cuts[i] = i - 1, the cost of cutting between all characters.

Every palindrome has a centre, either a character or a gap between two. Process centres from left to right; for each, grow the window outwards while the two end characters match. For every palindrome s[l..r] found, relax cuts[r + 1] with cuts[l] + 1. Because every palindrome ending before position l has its centre to the left of the current one, cuts[l] is already final when it is used. Total work is O(n²) with only O(n) memory, versus O(n²) memory for a full palindrome table.

title: Critical Connections in a Network
desc:
A network has n servers numbered 0 to n - 1, joined by undirected cables. connections[i] = [a, b] is a cable between servers a and b. Every server can reach every other server, directly or through other servers.

A cable is critical if removing it (and only it) leaves at least one pair of servers unable to reach each other.

Return all critical cables. Write each one as [a, b] with a < b. The rows may be listed in any order. If none is critical, return an empty list.
constraints: connections[i] = [a, b] with 0 ≤ a, b < n and a ≠ b
No pair of servers is joined by more than one cable
hints: A critical cable is a bridge. Trying to delete every edge and re-check connectivity costs O(E · (V + E)), which is too slow for large inputs.
Run a DFS and record for each node the time at which it was first visited. Then ask: from the subtree below an edge, can any node reach back to an ancestor above that edge?
Keep low[v], the smallest discovery time reachable from v's subtree using at most one back edge. A tree edge (u, v) is a bridge exactly when low[v] > disc[u].
editorial: Run a depth-first search that assigns each node a discovery time disc and computes low[v] = the smallest discovery time reachable from v's DFS subtree through tree edges followed by at most one non-tree (back) edge. When processing the child v of u over tree edge (u, v), after finishing v set low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). For any other already-visited neighbour w (not the parent edge), set low[u] = min(low[u], disc[w]).

The edge (u, v) is a bridge exactly when low[v] > disc[u]: nothing in v's subtree can climb back to u or above, so the cable is the only link. This is Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm, linear in nodes plus edges. Since depth can reach 1,000, an explicit stack (iterative DFS) avoids recursion limits. Normalise each bridge to [min, max] before returning.
solution:
def criticalConnections(n, connections):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(connections):
        adj[a].append((b, i))
        adj[b].append((a, i))
    disc = [-1] * n
    low = [0] * n
    out = []
    timer = 0
    disc[0] = low[0] = 0
    timer = 1
    stack = [(0, -1, 0)]  # node, edge id used to arrive, next neighbour index
    while stack:
        u, pe, k = stack.pop()
        if k < len(adj[u]):
            stack.append((u, pe, k + 1))
            v, eid = adj[u][k]
            if eid == pe:
                continue
            if disc[v] == -1:
                disc[v] = low[v] = timer
                timer += 1
                stack.append((v, eid, 0))
            else:
                low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v])
        elif stack:
            p = stack[-1][0]
            low[p] = min(low[p], low[u])
            if low[u] > disc[p]:
                out.append([min(p, u), max(p, u)])
    return out
